item.title: Apple is killing its Support Community forum next week (170 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theverge.com/tech/1031507/apple-community-support-forum-shutting-down, See on Hacker News

Jess Weatherbed

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

It’s the end of the road for the Apple Support Community. The dedicated discussion forum, which gave Apple users a place to exchange advice, troubleshoot, and generally chat about Apple products, has been placed into read-only mode, with a message from the company announcing that the Support Community will shut down for good on November 20th.

Here’s the full banner notice that’s currently displayed on the website:

“The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”

The Apple Support Community has undergone several name changes over the years, but its history as an online forum for providing user-to-user tech support goes back to 1998, when it first launched as the Apple Tech Exchange. Apple hasn’t specified what will happen to the decades worth of Support Community posts when the platform shuts down next week. Presumably, they’ll all disappear with it.

In a statement to MacRumors, Apple said it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs. We have reached out to Apple for comment.

item.title: I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you (219 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.theverge.com/tech/1012372/tv-privacy-acr-questions, See on Hacker News

Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.

To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.

Company representatives providing responses

Amazon: Eric Sveum, PR manager

Apple: Emily Ewing, public relations manager

Google: Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson

LG Electronics: Chris De Maria, director of public relations

Roku: Sarah Novatt, spokesperson

Samsung: Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager

TCL: Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events

One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)

As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.

Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.

Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.

1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?

Amazon:

No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.

Apple:

Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.

Google:

If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.

Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.

Samsung:

No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.

The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

2. Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?

Amazon:

Apple:

Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Google:

[Recorded audio and/or transcripts based on audio are] stored only if ‘Voice & Audio Activity’ (VAA) is explicitly enabled under Google Account Web & App Activity. Voice & Audio Activity is off by default. If VAA is off, voice requests are processed in real-time and not saved to the Google Account.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

If voice recognition is enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control’s microphone button or using the wake word), certain information generated as part of a specific voice recognition interaction may be stored locally on the TV to support voice-related features. Depending on the interaction, this may include Speech-to-text results derived from a user’s voice command.

Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, captured audio is promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Voice commands made via voice-enabled remotes may be retained to improve voice features and provide support, consistent with Roku’s privacy policy. Users can opt out in their Roku account privacy settings.

Samsung:

No. Samsung Smart TVs do not store voice recordings or transcripts on the device.

However, on secure servers, voice commands and transcripts are stored only to process requests and improve voice assistant services.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL does not collect audio data from TCL TV or remote microphones, or from the use of third-party voice features.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?

Amazon:

When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.

Apple:

Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.

For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.

Google:

If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes, but only if voice recognition has been enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control microphone button or using the wake word). When voice recognition is activated, the TV displays an on-screen indication that voice recognition is active and listening for the user’s command. Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku TVs don’t have microphones. Voice-enabled remotes let people control their Roku devices by voice, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No, for ambient or background listening. Samsung TVs do not passively monitor, record, or transmit audio from your home. Audio is only captured and transmitted when you actively initiate a voice command (such as pressing the microphone button on your remote or using the wake word). This voice input is processed securely to fulfill your requests, improve services, and support connected features under our voice privacy policies.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

4. Do your TVs collect any screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching?

Amazon:

Apple:

Apple TV 4K does not use automatic content recognition (ACR), nor does it collect screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers are watching. If a user chooses to ask a question about what’s on their screen, that data is processed by Siri AI. This feature is only initiated by a direct user request.

Google:

Google TV platform software does not utilize Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to capture on-screen video or screenshots. (Note: Third-party TV hardware OEMs may install separate ACR software, but Google TV OS itself does not).

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

No. ACR in LG TVs does not collect or store screenshots, screen images, screen recordings, or video recordings from the TV. Instead, it uses audio fingerprints generated from content audio using the TV’s internal soundboard (not a speaker) to identify the content being viewed.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Samsung:

No. Samsung TVs do not capture or store screenshots, screen recordings, or video recordings of what viewers watch.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

5. Do your TVs store or transmit data on what content viewers watch or listen to through the TV?

Amazon:

Yes. For example, customers can opt in to allow Fire TV to collect certain viewing information like what shows they’ve watched in third-party apps to improve and personalize their experience, including by displaying shows and movies in a Continue Watching row on the Fire TV home screen. Customers can manage that setting anytime via their device’s Privacy Settings.

Apple:

Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] stores and transmits viewing history, watchlists, and app interactions for rentals/purchases on GTV and FreePlay. We do not have viewing history on third party apps.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

If the user has agreed to the Viewing Information Agreement, viewing information may be collected or processed in certain circumstances, including the following:

- ACR: Where ACR is available and enabled, ACR-related information may be collected and processed to identify content being viewed from supported sources. ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology to identify content rather than collecting screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV. To operate ACR services, LG may process content-identification fingerprints together with device information, content source information, network information, and consent settings needed to support the feature. ACR is optional and is turned off by default, and users can disable the feature at any time through the TV settings. ACR does not operate within third-party streaming apps.

- LG Channels: When a user streams content through LG Channels, information about the content being viewed is processed and sent to our servers so we can provide the requested streaming service.

- Voice Recognition: When users make voice commands, those commands and current viewing information (such as channel number and program name, and whether the source is an antenna or set-top-box) are sent to the server to process the voice commands and provide appropriate responses.

- Usage Information: Certain viewing information may also be collected as part of usage information relating to how the user interacts with the TV and its services, such as information about content selected for viewing or channels the user switches to.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

We collect streaming activity as described in our privacy policy. Smart TV Experience, which can identify other content on screen, is off by default in the US and is enabled only if the user opts in.

Samsung:

Yes, but only for TV programming and app viewing history. Samsung TVs do not monitor or transmit your personal files or private media.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL collects limited data only for diagnostics and product improvement from some models of TCL Smart TVs. This collection is disclosed to users at setup and in TCL’s privacy notice, uses pseudonymization to prevent user profiling, and can be turned off by the user.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

6. Do your TVs collect any telemetry about where users are clicking, selecting, tapping, or otherwise looking when using the TV?

Amazon:

Fire TV collects data about how customers use the device, such as navigating the home screen or opening apps, to provide and improve features. Customers can opt out of certain data collection and use via Privacy Settings.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] collects device navigation telemetry (button presses, navigation clicks, app launch/exit events) under ‘Usage & Diagnostics’ settings to assess system health and reliability. Does not store “hovering” or “highlight” states.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

To provide and improve smart services, the LG smart TV may collect certain basic usage information about how users interact with the TV, such as the features, menu items, apps, or services they select or use. LG does not collect information about a user’s activity within third-party apps. LG does not track where users are looking when using the TV.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

We collect standard usage data, such as button presses and menu selections, to run and improve the product.

Samsung:

For menu interactions and viewing selections, interactions (like clicks or selections) are analyzed primarily in aggregate to improve the user experience and service recommendations.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL does not collect data at the device level regarding what viewers watch, except when a user requests remote diagnostic support, in which case the information is used to fix the problem the user reported.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

7. Do your TVs transmit any information that could identify the location of their owner, including their public IP address, Wi-Fi network SSID, GPS coordinates, and/or actual street address?

Amazon:

Yes. For example, IP addresses are transmitted as part of normal network communication, for your device to communicate with the internet and deliver content. There is no GPS hardware on Fire TV devices.

Apple:

Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] transmits public IP address, Wi-Fi scan data (SSID/BSSID), and account/device regional configuration to determine approximate or precise device location.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

To provide Smart TV functionality, the TV must be connected to the internet. If the TV is connected to the internet, then like any other internet-connected device, the Smart TV will transmit its IP address. The IP address may be used to determine its approximate geographic location to provide services appropriate for the user’s region.

Separately, when ACR is enabled, the TV’s IP address and information about nearby Wi-Fi networks, such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may be used to estimate the TV’s approximate location as part of the ACR service. This ACR-related location processing is limited to ACR and is not used generally across other TV services.

The TV does not contain a GPS module and does not use GPS to determine its location.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku TVs don’t collect GPS data. Like any connected device, they transmit a public IP address, which may be used for approximate location, among other purposes, per our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No, for physical locations. Samsung TVs do not collect or transmit GPS coordinates, Wi-Fi SSIDs, or your physical street address. However, for network connection, the TV must transmit its public IP address to connect to the internet and run basic features (like the Smart Hub and software updates). This IP address is only used for network communication and general region detection (like country or state), not to pinpoint your actual address.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

To provide location-based services, TCL collects IP address and Wi-Fi network name (SSID) information, as described in the terms and privacy policy to which users agree when they initially set up their TV. TCL uses this information only to identify a country or city in order to deliver services, not the user’s specific location. TCL TVs have no GPS modules, and TCL does not collect street addresses through the TV. If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

8. Do your TVs store or transmit any other potentially personally identifying information about their owners, including their name, age, gender, orientation, and demographic?

Amazon:

Fire TV devices are associated with customers’ Amazon account, which includes their name and account information.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Because Google TV requires a Google Account for smart functionality, linked profile information (name, email, age, gender) is accessed, stored, and transmitted for personalization and age-restriction policies.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

When creating an LG account, the user provides their name, email address and date of birth (to confirm applicable age requirements). If a user creates an LG account from their Smart TV, the TV will temporarily store and then transmit this information to LG’s servers.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Users provide account information, such as name and email, when they create a Roku account, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

Samsung SmartTVs do not collect/store or transmit name, age, gender, orientation or demographic information.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

If a user creates a TCL account on a TCL Google TV, TCL collects an email address and age to confirm that the user is an adult. Apart from that, TCL’s practice is not to collect personally identifiable information from its televisions.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

9. Does your company store any of the kinds of information in Question 7 or 8 in the cloud or other remote servers? If so, which?

Amazon:

Yes. Information transmitted to Amazon’s cloud is encrypted in transit and stored securely.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Both location data (IP address/Wi-Fi) and Google Account profile data (name, email address, age/gender demographics) are stored on Google’s cloud servers linked to your account profile.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes. Information such as IP addresses, device-level identifiers, and, if a user has an LG Account, account information such as name, email address, and date of birth, is stored on LG’s cloud or other remote servers. When ACR is enabled, the ACR-related information described above, including nearby Wi-Fi network information such as MAC addresses and signal strength, may also be stored on remote servers.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Data may be stored on Roku’s servers or with major cloud providers to operate the service, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

Yes. The information described above is stored in encrypted or hashed form within secure cloud infrastructure managed by Samsung.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

The limited information described above is stored with cloud service providers, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, subject to TCL’s terms and privacy policy.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

10. Do your TVs transmit any information about the other devices on an owner’s home Wi-Fi network?

Amazon:

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

[Google TV] discovers nearby Cast-enabled devices and smart home hardware via local network protocols (mDNS, SSDP, Matter/Thread) and transmits device discovery/connectivity logs.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

To support connectivity capabilities, LG smart TVs identify other devices on the user’s Wi-Fi network. Where necessary to support device-discovery functionality, information about nearby devices detected on the local network may be transmitted to a third-party service provider acting on LG’s behalf to identify compatible devices.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku TVs may detect other devices on the home network to support features like AirPlay, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No. Samsung TVs do not scan your home Wi-Fi network to collect or transmit an inventory of other connected devices. The TV only communicates with compatible devices that customers actively choose to connect (such as for casting or via the SmartThings app under their Samsung Account) to provide smart home control, not to monitor other devices on your network.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Users may connect their TCL Smart TV to other devices so they can control those devices. For some on-device functions, such as screen casting or connecting devices to each other, the TV may detect other devices on the same Wi-Fi network. That data is normally exchanged only between the devices. If a connection problem occurs, diagnostics may report the name of the device involved. When a consumer chooses to control the TV through a voice service such as Amazon Alexa, data is exchanged between the TV, TCL’s cloud, and Amazon so the service can function.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

11. Can users entirely opt out of transmitting all forms of data?

Amazon:

No. Basic functionality like downloading apps and streaming content requires transmitting data. However, Fire TV does provide customers the ability to control the collection or transmission of certain data, including data about the frequency and duration of use of third-party apps and about what customers have watched in third-party apps.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Users cannot opt out of 100% of data transmission while connected to the internet. Essential system telemetry (device model, OS version, activation status, security updates) is mandatory for basic operation.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Users can stop the transmission of personal data associated with smart TV services by withdrawing their acceptance of the Privacy Policy or Terms of Use. If they do so, smart TV services will no longer be available, and the data transmission required to provide those services will cease. The TV can still be used for basic functions that do not require smart TV services, such as Live TV or HDMI inputs.

Users can also separately choose whether to use optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising. These features require separate agreements and can be reviewed, managed, or withdrawn through the TV settings at any time. Declining or withdrawing these optional agreements does not prevent users from using core smart TV functionality.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

No, but Roku offers privacy settings for voice data, Smart TV Experience, and ad personalization.

Samsung:

No, not all forms. At minimum, data is needed to run a digital platform (e.g. to provide the service and security).

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Some data is transmitted to TCL because the Smart TV services and functions the user chooses depend on such data. Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

12. Are users automatically opted out by default when setting up the TV?

Amazon:

Customers are not opted out of all data transmission by default. Again, basic device functionality requires data to be transmitted. However, there are some Fire TV features like Automatic Content Recognition that are default off and that customers must affirmatively turn on in order to allow those features to work and transmit data.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

During initial setup, options such as Usage & Diagnostics sharing, personalized recommendations/ads, and Google Account Web & App Activity tracking are enabled by default unless opted out.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes. Users can choose to opt-in by accepting each applicable agreement before the relevant services or features are enabled. Optional features such as voice recognition, ACR, and interest-based advertising are not enabled by default . Users can also manage or withdraw their consent through the TV settings at any time.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Smart TV Experience is off by default in the US.

Samsung:

Yes. For Viewing Information Services (VIS), which includes Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), consumers are opted out by default and must affirmatively enable it.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

Users can opt out of sending TCL the limited interaction data collected for diagnostics and product improvement.

The ACR technology on those TCL Smart TVs which support that feature comes from the operating system provider or third-party software providers. Users choose whether to turn on ACR when they first set up the TV, and they can turn it off at any time in the ACR provider’s privacy settings. Before ACR is turned on, the user must agree to the ACR provider’s terms and conditions. Those terms and privacy policies explain what viewing data the provider may store or transmit with the user’s consent.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

13. If users opt out, does the TV store any of these forms of data internally for potential use at a later date?

Amazon:

No. If a customer has opted out of Fire TV collecting data, that data will not be collected unless the customer re-enables collection.

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

If cloud tracking is disabled, local temporary caches and system operational buffers remain on-device for immediate system execution and local performance before deletion.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

No. If a user withdraws consent under an applicable agreement, data previously collected under that agreement is handled in accordance with LG’s applicable data retention and deletion policies, including deletion or anonymization where appropriate, and is not retained for potential future use.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

Roku’s ad personalization setting affects which ads users see. Data is still collected and used for other purposes, as described in our privacy policy.

Samsung:

No. If users opt out, the TV stops collecting new viewing data immediately and does not store it internally for later use. Once you disable the Viewing Information Services (VIS), any previously collected ACR data is deleted from our servers and can no longer be associated with your device.

Sony:

Sony did not provide an answer to this question.

TCL:

TCL did not provide a direct answer to this question.

Vizio:

Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

14. Does disconnecting a TV from the internet prevent all these forms of data transmission?

Amazon:

Apple:

Apple did not provide an answer to this question.

Google:

Severing internet access (disconnecting Wi-Fi or removing Ethernet) halts all outbound external data transmission to Google cloud servers. Of course this also stops any streaming service from operating.

Hisense:

Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.

LG:

Yes. A TV must be connected to the internet to transmit data. For voice recognition specifically, voice data is not stored for later upload when the TV is offline and is not transmitted when the connection is restored.

Panasonic:

Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.

Roku:

item.title: Open research, stronger privacy: Making Firefox users harder to fingerprint (128 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.mozilla.org/security/2026/11/10/open-research-stronger-privacy-making-firefox-users-harder-to-fingerprint/, See on Hacker News

Firefox is strengthening protection against trackers that recognize you across websites, even when they don’t use cookies. The latest fingerprinting protections shipped in Firefox reduce the extractable distinguishing details, making more Firefox users look alike to tracking scripts and strengthening individuals’ privacy in everyday browsing.

These protections build on our research into browser and device fingerprinting, a technique that combines details about your browser and device to identify you across websites. We investigated which details contribute most to make users uniquely identifiable, turned those findings into practical protections for Firefox users, and shared our results openly so the wider web security and privacy community can build stronger defenses.

Our findings are documented in the research paper Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild, which has been accepted for publication at Computer and Communications Security (CCS) 2026, a leading international conference on computer security and privacy. We’ve also created an easier-to-digest website and browser test suite to help explore the findings in the paper.

Cookie-less Tracking

Browser fingerprinting combines details about your browser and device, such as available fonts, screen dimensions, and graphics hardware, to build a uniquely recognizable profile. Each piece may seem ordinary, but together, they can enable trackers to single you out across websites, even without storing a cookie.

Effective fingerprinting protection starts with understanding which browser details trackers rely on most. Our research found that protecting just a handful of browser features can significantly weaken popular fingerprinting techniques. That finding enabled us to focus on Firefox’s protections where they can make the biggest difference and bring those benefits to all Firefox users.

To evaluate these techniques, we simulated the browser measurements collected by fingerprinting scripts from Fingerprint Pro, Signifyd, and Akamai and examined how their combinations distinguish users. The study used measurements collected from nearly 25 million Firefox users, with additional privacy safeguards beyond Mozilla’s existing data collection policies.

Those safeguards included OHTTP, which routed encrypted requests through a relay. The relay sees the user’s IP address but not the request contents, while Mozilla receives the contents without the user’s IP address. We also tightly limited data access and retention: individual telemetry records were deleted several months ago and only aggregate results were retained and published for open science. Our research paper explains the method, safeguards and ethical considerations in detail.

Less distinctive, more private

Our approach reduces unnecessary differences in the information Firefox exposes to websites. For example, Firefox limits the information exposed through screen resolution APIs to hide the size and position of the system taskbar or dock, preventing that desktop layout detail from contributing to a fingerprint. As another example, it can report processor counts as either 4 or 8 instead of exposing the exact count, which can make a browser more distinctive.

Our goal is to make more users’ browsers look similar to fingerprinting scripts while preserving the information websites need to function correctly, like language and timezone settings. Firefox also uses randomization to make other fingerprinting signals less useful to trackers, though the benefits of these techniques are harder to quantify and fall outside the measurements reported here.

In our evaluation, these protections (the most recent of which shipped in Firefox 145) substantially degraded the precision of fingerprinting in Firefox both by reducing the number of users with unique fingerprints and increasing the size of the groups of users that share a fingerprint.

The research also enabled us to identify why certain measurements differed between users. Addressing these differences produced more consistent outputs for image rendering, Web Audio, and mathematical operations on Android, reducing the distinguishing details available to fingerprinters.

These results show that substantial reductions in browser fingerprint uniqueness are achievable and provide meaningful progress toward stronger online privacy. These do not make fingerprinting impossible as trackers can surely adapt. But our research provides a concrete, measurable improvement in browser defenses against online tracking.

The built-in privacy protections in Firefox are complemented with capabilities and options to further strengthen the protection against online fingerprinters. Built-in and always-on Total Cookie Protection in Firefox segments stateful identifiers and prevents trackers from following you across your browsing using cookies. Firefox Relay provides you with unique email masks, preventing websites from linking your subscriptions to other sites via data brokers. And Firefox now integrates a free VPN that masks your IP address to protect against tracking and fingerprinting. Together with Firefox’s enhanced fingerprinting protections, these capabilities provide everyone a very strong foundation to take back control of their privacy online.

Research that improves everyday browsing

Privacy protections need to work on the websites people use every day. These findings allow us to prioritize changes that deliver measurable privacy benefits while keeping those websites working.

Some of Firefox’s fingerprinting protections, such as hiding the size of your taskbar or dock, are on by default in all browsing modes. Others are introduced first in Private Browsing and Strict Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) mode, while we work toward enabling them by default, following the same strategy we’ve used for years. To enable these additional protections in all your Firefox windows, select Strict in the Enhanced Tracking Protection settings. Follow the steps here if the “Strict” protections get in the way of any website functionality.

Want to explore browser fingerprinting yourself? Visit the research project page to try the fingerprinting test and learn more about our findings. For a closer look at what we measured and how we turned those insights into Firefox protections, explore our paper: Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild.

We’ll keep strengthening Firefox’s privacy protections while continuing to work in the open. By sharing our research, our code, and what we learn, we’re shaping the web we envision: free, private, secure, and accessible to all.

item.title: Can a Linear Program Do Weight-Space Programming? (164 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://nathan.rs/posts/weight-space-lp/, See on Hacker News

Last week, MIT CSAIL published Sparks of Weight-Space Programming. Given the raw weights of a small network, GPT-6 Astra could tell which game it had been trained to play. Given only a game’s rules, it could write the weights of a small network from scratch and beat networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. No gradients, no training loop, just reasoning about what the weights compute. They coined this weight-space programming.

In another experiment, they asked Astra to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math by editing its weights. Astra changed only 0.016% of the weights, and MATH-500 accuracy jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%.1

Looking at Astra’s edit, I realized most of its search was solving a linear program by trial and error. It spent about 8 hours and 28 forward passes choosing which weights to change and by how much. A couple of LP solves, about a minute each, do the same job with 8× fewer changed weights. In this post I’ll walk through the edit, why it’s an LP, and what that says about the fix itself.

Thinking loops#

Small reasoning models have a common failure: they get stuck in thinking loops, repeating the same few lines over and over instead of finishing their reasoning. Qwen3.5-0.8B is especially prone to it, and its model card says so. On MATH-500, 93% of the base model’s answers ran into the 32,768-token limit without ever reaching an answer.

The edit fixes the loops, so it helps anywhere the model loops. That includes instruction following: IFEval went from 21% to 62%.

Qwen3.5-0.8BMATH-500GSM8KIFEvalHit token limit
Base7.913.821.093.0%
Astra’s edit48.167.162.333.1%

On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, Astra couldn’t meaningfully improve its math ability. As the authors put it, editing the weights could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but couldn’t add one the model lacked.

How Astra fixed the loops#

Transformers use residual connections: each layer’s output is added to its input rather than replacing it. Follow one token through the network and you get a single vector that every layer adds to, called the residual stream (1,024-dimensional in this model). When the model is looping, the residual stream shifts in a consistent direction. Astra’s fix was to edit two layers so that what they add points the opposite way.

Finding the loop direction#

Astra wrote four pairs of short texts, each a piece of productive reasoning and a looping version of the same reasoning. It ran all eight through the model and recorded each token’s residual stream vector at one layer. Averaging over the looping texts gives one vector, and averaging over the productive texts gives another. Their difference, normalized, is the loop direction $u$: the way the residual stream moves when the model loops.

Editing the weights#

Each MLP ends with a matrix $W$ (called down_proj). At every token, it turns the MLP’s 3,584-dimensional hidden activation $h$ into a 1,024-dimensional output $Wh$, which gets added to the residual stream $x$:

$$x \leftarrow x + Wh, \qquad Wh = \sum_j h_j \, w_j$$

So the MLP’s output is always a weighted sum of the same 3,584 vectors, the columns $w_j$ of $W$. $W$ fixes what those vectors are; the activations $h_j$ decide how much of each one gets added at each token.

Each column points partly along $u$. That amount, $u^\top w_j$, is how much column $j$ pushes the model toward looping whenever $h_j$ is active. Astra’s edit subtracts a multiple $\alpha$ of it:

$$w_j \to w_j - \alpha \, (u^\top w_j) \, u$$

At $\alpha = 1$ the component along $u$ is gone, so the column no longer pushes toward looping. Doing this to every column in layers 15 and 19 took accuracy from 9% to 33% on GSM8K and MATH training problems. At $\alpha = 6$ the component is flipped: a column that wrote $+a$ along $u$ now writes $-5a$, and pushes the model away from looping whenever it’s used.

Every edited column changes by a multiple of the same vector $u$. So the whole edit is one direction $u$ plus one number per column, $v_j = -\alpha\,(u^\top w_j)$, which is zero for columns left alone. That’s a rank-1 change:

$$\Delta W = u\,v^\top$$

At each token, it adds $(v \cdot h_t)\,u$ to the residual stream: some amount of $u$, set by how active the edited columns are. No other direction changes.

That leaves $v$ to choose: which columns to edit, and how large $\alpha$ should be. Astra worked it out by trial and error, testing each edit on a fresh batch of those training problems:

Edit on layers 15 and 19Accuracy
Base model~9%
Every column, α = 133%
Every column, α = 243%
Every column, α = 348%
Random direction (control)12.5%
Top 64 columns, α = 655%

Pushing harder than $\alpha = 1$ helped more, and a random direction did nothing. The final edit used $\alpha = 6$ on only the 64 columns per layer that wrote the most $u$ on looping text.

Where the time went#

The paper released Astra’s full logs: every tool call, every forward pass, every note it wrote to itself. Astra had a Python kernel with the weights loaded and a budget of 50 forward passes, each a batched run of the model on training problems or texts of its choosing.

The edit was frozen after about 10 hours, and the last 17 passes re-tested it without changing anything.2 Of those 10 hours, finding $u$ took 15 minutes. Finding $v$ took about 8 hours.

Choosing v is a linear program#

Astra was searching for a $v$ that strongly pushes looping tokens away from $u$ while barely touching productive ones. Since the push at token $t$ is $v \cdot h_t$, linear in $v$, both requirements are linear inequalities.

I labeled tokens from the base model’s own traces: looping tokens ($R$), deep inside a loop, and productive tokens ($P$), well before any loop starts,3 and recorded their activations $h_t$ at layers 15 and 19. Each one becomes a constraint, and the LP picks the $v$ with the smallest L1 norm $\sum_j |v_j|$:

$$ \begin{aligned} \min_v \quad & \sum_j |v_j| \\ \text{s.t.} \quad & v \cdot h_t \le -\delta && t \in R \quad \text{(at least } \delta \text{ away from } u\text{)} \\ & |v \cdot h_t| \le \varepsilon && t \in P \quad \text{(at most } \varepsilon\text{)} \end{aligned} $$

In practice no $v$ satisfies every constraint, so each one gets a penalized slack variable.

Minimizing L1 tends to make $v$ sparse. The L1 ball is a diamond, and when you grow it until it touches the feasible region, it usually touches at a corner, where most coordinates are exactly zero. So the LP picks the columns as well as the amounts.

To get exactly 8 columns per layer, I kept the 8 with the largest effect and solved again with the rest fixed at zero.4

That replaces Astra’s 8-hour search, including its choice of columns and $\alpha$, with a couple of LP solves. An off-the-shelf solver (HiGHS) took over 20 minutes each on these constraints, so I wrote a GPU solver (PDHG, the algorithm behind PDLP) that gets within 0.2% of its optimum in about a minute.5

Results#

I tested two LP edits. Both use Astra’s layers. One uses Astra’s direction $u$. The other uses a heuristic direction: label tokens in the model’s own traces as looping or productive with a simple repetition detector, then take the difference of their average residual streams. It’s the same recipe Astra used, minus the hand-written texts, so no LLM is involved. I tuned the LP’s settings on a separate 128-problem dev set; everything in the chart and table is on data never used for fitting or tuning.

Changed weightsGSM8K testMATH-500IFEval
Base model014.17.022.9
Astra’s edit130,18868.250.961.9
LP, Astra’s direction16,29169.651.759.7
LP, heuristic direction16,27165.447.860.4

With Astra’s direction, the LP matches Astra’s edit on every benchmark, within noise, while changing 8× fewer weights. With the heuristic direction, it gets about 93% of the way there.

A few other things showed up:

  • The search mattered, and the LP replaces it. On the dev set, reusing Astra’s recipe (top 64 columns, $\alpha = 6$) on the heuristic direction without searching again scores 44.5. The LP scores 54.7.
  • Different columns, same fix. The LP’s 8 columns share only 3 (layer 15) and 1 (layer 19) with Astra’s 64. Many sparse solutions work; what matters is the total push along $u.$
  • A random direction does nothing. On the dev set, a random $u$ of the same size scores 10.2, against 10.9 for the base model.

A steering vector does the same job#

An edit can only tell a looping token apart from a productive one through its activations, and a loop isn’t recognizable from them until it’s well under way.6 So on the dev set, asking the LP to push only on loop-like tokens did no better than pushing on every token.

The LP’s 8 columns in layer 15 are active on 89% of tokens, and the push they add barely varies from token to token, so the edit is close to a constant push along $u$. A constant push doesn’t need a weight edit. It can be added directly as a steering vector, a fixed vector added to the residual stream at every token.

The table below adds the LP edit’s average push along $u$ to the unedited model at layers 15 and 19, at three strengths:

Steering strength (× the LP edit’s average push)Dev setMATH-500
0.5×51.6
1×57.850.8
2×31.2

For comparison, on the same runs: the LP edit scores 62.5 on the dev set and 53.2 on MATH-500, Astra’s edit 59.4 and 50.0, the base model 10.9 and 7.0. MATH-500 here is one sample per problem.

At 1×, the steering vector recovers essentially the whole fix. The window is narrow: at 0.5× the loops come back, and at 2× they stop but the reasoning falls apart.

The only difference is delivery. The LP edit is an ordinary checkpoint; the steering vector needs extra code at inference time.

Limitations and what’s next#

This is one model. The LP still relies on Astra for the layers, and the best results use Astra’s direction too. The heuristic direction gets most of the way without an LLM, but not all of it.

Loops also turned out to be fixable with a constant push, so the LP’s per-token constraints didn’t end up mattering much. A behavior that should change some tokens and leave others alone would be a better test of them. Choosing the layers without an agent is the other open piece.

Lastly, this was only tested on removing loops. Many other behaviors, like refusal or sycophancy, can be steered by adding or removing a single direction in the residual stream.7 If a behavior can be steered with one direction, choosing how to build it into the weights should be the same LP, but that still needs testing.

Code, edits, and the full write-up are on GitHub.

Citation#

item.description:
URL: https://www.experimental-history.com/p/we-need-more-goat-sacrifices, See on Hacker News

Just a quick thing before this week’s post. If you’ve preordered THE STRANGEST IDEA IN THE WORLD, I’d like to send you a little something extra in the mail. Submit your preorder receipt and your mailing address here. This is only available to folks with US or UK addresses—apologies to those who live elsewhere! In the US, everyone with a valid entry will get one; in the UK they’ll pick winners randomly. The link will be open until December 11, and we’ll start mailing things out after that. I won’t spoil the surprise, but I will say that a) it’s very silly, and b) I can’t wait to get mine.

(For the US: US Residents, 18+. Ends December 11, 2026. See terms at https://sites.prh.com/strangestidea-preorder)

Anyway, onto the post!

Before anybody enacts a major social policy or launches any philanthropic programs, they should sacrifice a goat. There ought to be an entire liturgy of grotesqueries, in fact—pricked fingers, names written in blood, robes, candles, chanting, obsidian blades, still-beating hearts, the whole shebang.

The point of this ritual is not to signal our obeisance to the gods (although if any of them want to stop by and help us out, that would be cool), but to remind ourselves that we know nothing. This is procedurally-induced humility, which is desperately necessary, because an alarming number of our best-intentioned interventions do not work.

For example:

  • In 2009, Congress spent $3 billion on “School Improvement Grants” for the worst-performing schools in the country. As far as we can tell, those grants did nothing.

  • Universities that hired a Chief Diversity Officer between 2001 and 2019 did not end up with more diverse students, faculties, or administrators.

  • The American government spent $280 million to help Afghan women get jobs, and now they can’t really say whether any women got any jobs.1

  • Remember 20 years ago, when giving laptops to kids in developing countries seemed like the most important thing to do? Well, a 10-year RCT of 531 rural schools in Peru found zero effects of “One Laptop Per Child” on academic performance.2

  • Researchers developed four different messages that were supposed to convince parents to vaccinate their kids. None of the messages worked, and one of them accidentally made parents more likely to believe that vaccines cause autism.

Most of those are left-coded failures, so here are some right-coded failures:

  • When Arkansas added a work requirement to Medicaid, the number of Arkansans with health insurance went down without any increase in employment.

  • In 2002, the Bush administration launched the Building Strong Families Program, which provided counseling to low-income, unmarried parents with the goal of strengthening their relationships, keeping them both in their child’s life, and ultimately getting them married. Three years later, an independent evaluation found that the program did none of those things.

  • And here is the effect of four different abstinence-only sex ed programs that run across the United States:

In the social sciences, nothing ever dies; it merely becomes embarrassing. We can’t say that it’s impossible for anything like these programs to ever succeed, given enough time, flimsy theorizing, and generous definitions of “success”. The point is that these effects should be large, and instead they are nonexistent. Seems to me like it’s time to get the goats in here.

It’s inevitable that some of our interventions are going to fail. (If they don’t, we should either be suspicious of the results, or we should be more ambitious with our programs.) What we really want to know is: when we try to improve the world through some policy or program, how often do we succeed?

We don’t have a good answer to this question, but we do have a good joke about it.

In 1987, the sociologist Peter Rossi wrote a tongue-in-cheek paper that accidentally became his intellectual legacy. He would later refer to it as “far from being one of my favorites” and “the source of considerable embarrassment”, and yet it’s the only thing of his that I’ve ever read or even heard of.3 It was called “The Iron Law of Evaluation and Other Metallic Rules“, and it went like this, lightly paraphrased:

  • The Iron Law of Evaluation: The net expected impact of a large social program is zero.

  • The Stainless Steel Law: Better-designed evaluations are more likely to find null effects.

  • The Brass Law: The more a program is intended to change people, the more likely the impact of that program will be zero.

  • The Zinc Law: The programs most likely to be evaluated are those most likely to fail.

Rossi tried to walk back his laws shortly before he died in 2006, insisting that there is now a “large number of well conducted impact assessments that yield statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”. Still, even after supposedly enduring 16 years of embarrassment from his one satirical paper, he concluded, “we really do not know whether programs over a wide variety of substantive areas are worth anything”.

Rossi did not do us the favor of actually naming any of those “statistically and substantively significant effect sizes”, and I know why, because I have gone looking for them, and they are not easy to find. The Earned Income Tax Credit, which is designed to benefit low- and middle-income families, was once considered a slam dunk; now a new analysis suggests that it might not do anything. Plain packaging—where you strip cigarette boxes of their attractive branding—seems like a no brainer, but in Australia, it looks like the policy caused smokers to switch to cheaper brands and to smoke more. There’s a reading and math program that has done well in India, but as soon as other researchers tried to implement it elsewhere, the effects shrank.

You can always find a one-off study showing that an intervention works, but if we’ve learned anything from the past 20 years of social science, it’s that one-off studies ain’t worth much. It’s so easy to juice your stats and journals are so hungry for positive results that entire literatures can be suspect, and decades of research can culminate in a shrug. “Sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t, it depends on all sorts of factors that we can’t really specify, so uh, good luck!”

Even if we take Rossi at his word and there are as-yet-unnamed programs out there that are reliable and effective, the question still remains: why aren’t there more of them? Why do so many of our best-laid plans end up like this:

The answer lies, I think, in a 50-year-old study that is almost certainly false.

One of my favorite genres of psychology experiment is called something like: “the study is probably bullshit but the effect is probably real”. At the top of that heap is The Illusion of Control, a classic from 1975 and a favorite of Psych 101 classes everywhere. Usually, this study gets summarized as “people value their lottery tickets more when you let them pick the numbers vs. when you pick the numbers for them.” It’s as if people think that the mere act of picking imbues their ticket with a bit of juju, which makes them less willing to part with it.

That would be a beautiful study, but it wasn’t the study that was actually conducted. The “lottery tickets” in question were in fact football cards, each one with a picture of a player, their team, etc. Some participants were given the opportunity to choose their football card and some had a card handed to them. Later, just before the drawing, all of the participants were asked how much it would take to buy their card back. On average, the pickers asked for $8.67, while the not-pickers said $1.86.4

I’m sure you can see the obvious and less exciting explanation for these results: when people were given the chance, they picked their favorite players. The people who didn’t get to pick ended up with a card they liked less. This “illusion of control” effect is merely a “reality of people having preferences and acting on them” effect.5

Unsurprisingly, well-powered, preregistered replications with actual lotteries have failed to find any difference in picking vs. not-picking. So that’s that: there’s no such thing as the illusion of control.

Except...obviously there’s an illusion of control! Look around! People will blow on their dice at the craps table, they’ll don their lucky undies when the Knicks go to the finals, they’ll scream “look out!” to the hapless protagonists of a horror movie. When I was a kid, my parents used to send me off to play arcade games without any quarters, knowing that I would simply move the joystick in synchrony with the demo playing on the screen, convincing myself that I was causing the characters to move, when in fact I was merely mirroring them.

Put it this way: why do you think The Secret has sold over 30 million copies? It ain’t the beautiful prose or the sterling scientific evidence. It’s because when Rhonda Byrne tells you that “your thoughts are the primary cause of everything,” it feels kind of true. After all, can’t you jinx yourself by thinking the wrong thing? Haven’t you ever been like “whatever you do, don’t spill this soup” and then the next thing you know you’ve got a shirtful of bisque? And if brainwaves are powerful enough to spill soup, who knows what else they might do!

So no, people don’t believe they can magically improve their chances of winning the lottery by picking the numbers themselves. Still, our intentions feel more potent than they should, and this shows up not only in our harmless superstitions, but also in the way we keep meddling in each other’s lives despite having no idea what we’re doing.6

How do I know my preferred policies will have their intended results? Well, because I intend them. That’s not really my answer to the question; it’s the reason I don’t even think of the question in the first place.

Here’s the real evidence of our illusion of control: we’re so certain our interventions will work that we forget to check whether they do at all.

For instance, the National Science Foundation funds over 1,000 STEM education projects, which are aimed at improving curricula, training, student outcomes, etc. According to an analysis by Stuart Buck, 76% of the time, the researchers running those programs don’t even attempt to evaluate them with actual experiments. Apparently if you have a bright idea about how to teach kindergarteners to code, you don’t need to bother assessing it. It turns out George W. Bush was actually right when he said:

Speaking of the government, according to a report from the Government Accountability Office, many federal programs don’t even define their goals, let alone collect data on their progress toward those goals. For instance, the Department of Homeland Security is supposed to stop people from producing and distributing illicit fentanyl, and so they do things like search people’s cars and walk around with drug-sniffing dogs. When DHS was asked, “How do we know any of this is working? What would success even look like?”, they were like “hmm great questions”. They hadn’t set any goals or collected any data, despite being required to do so by law. As the GAO puts it with characteristic mildness: “As a result, DHS’s ability to fully understand the effectiveness of these efforts is limited.”

Maybe it’s too much to expect that the Department of Homeland Security, especially in its current incarnation, would try to figure out whether it’s doing things that actually work. But it’s certainly not too much to expect of private philanthropists, who choose to give away their money of their own free will. Certainly they would care whether their dollars do anything. Right?

Wrong. In 2018, Kenneth Langone, the Home Depot billionaire, donated $100 million to eliminate tuition fees at New York University’s main medical school. This was supposed to encourage med students to pick lower-paying specialties like pediatrics and primary care, and it was supposed to attract lower-income students to medical school in the first place. But neither of those things happened. The makeup of the student body hasn’t changed, and they’re picking the same specialities they always did.

In this case, it should have been easy to foresee that those beaucoup bucks were going to do bupkis. First, medical school is already a good investment, regardless of income: yes, you take on a big pile of debt, but you also make a much bigger pile of money, even in the lowest-compensated specialties. Second, wiping out that debt does almost nothing to reduce the disparities between specialties: the average orthopedic surgeon earns $564,000 per year, while the average family practitioner earns about $281,000. If both of them work for 30 years, the surgeon earns about $17 million, while the family doc earns about $8 million. Meanwhile, the average medical school debt is about $200k, which is nothing compared to an extra $9 million over the course of your lifetime.

And remember: in this situation, both the surgeon and the family doc attend for free, regardless of how much money they had when they arrived, or how much money they make after they leave. So there’s no reason why free tuition should encourage anybody to do anything differently—except to apply to NYU in the first place. And indeed, applications are up 47%.7

To be clear, giving away dunderheaded donations is better than a lot of things that billionaires could be doing with their money, like buying a second superyacht or digging an additional doomsday bunker so they have a place to summer after the apocalypse. I’m glad that the plutocrats are trying to do something nice. I would just like them to succeed.

When people see our big heap of failed interventions, they tend to go through three stages of grief.

  1. Bargaining

Okay, fine, these high-minded, utopian interventions don’t work, so what we really need is Common Sense and Obviously Good Ideas. For example, if you want to make poor people better off, you should give them money. That’s just Common Sense! That’s an Obviously Good Idea!

Unfortunately, large, well-designed randomized controlled trials keep finding null effects of unconditional cash transfers. In one study, when low-income participants got $2000 with no strings attached, it made them less happy compared to people who got $500 or nothing at all. Psychologically, receiving 20 Benjamins was about 25% as bad as losing your job during the pandemic. That finding might be a fluke, but it also showed up in a study where researchers wiped out a bunch of people’s medical debt and it maybe made them more depressed.

These programs do succeed in sense that when you give people more money, they have more money, and they spend it on things that they need. It’s just surprisingly difficult to find any evidence that having more money makes a difference. (Though note that results are more promising in low- and middle- income countries.)

  1. Denial

This is where people typically raise the no true Scotsman defense: if we get bad results from a good idea, it must be because someone screwed something up, not because the good ideas were actually bad ideas. Maybe the measures were wrong, the implementation was shoddy, or the people who benefitted didn’t fill out the followup survey for some reason.

This response isn’t totally irrational; programs go pear-shaped all the time. Maybe your One Laptop Per Child program only failed because all the laptops got stolen out of the back of the truck. Case in point: in that medical debt study, it seems like 76% of people didn’t even realize their medical debt had been wiped out. (But don’t get too excited: if anything, calling people and informing them of this boon made them slightly more depressed.)

The real problem with no-true-Scotsman-ing these studies is that you must subscribe to the dubious belief that some tiny tweaks will somehow unlock giant effects. This is a holdover from pre-replication-crisis psychology, back when we thought you could, say, subliminally flash an American flag at someone and make them more likely to vote for a Republican two weeks later. It now seems like rinky-dink interventions tend to have rinky-dink effects, or none at all. So yes, we could always pick more appropriate measures, and the facilitators delivering the intervention could always have a bit more pep in their step. That might be enough to make a program slightly more effective, but it’s not enough to turn a null result into a blockbuster.

  1. Acceptance

Acceptance sounds good, but it isn’t. Once we realize how hard it is to improve people’s lives, it’s tempting to believe that doing so is simply impossible, and so we are excused from even trying.

This is a bit like finding out that bloodletting doesn’t work and then concluding that no medicine can ever work. (“Well, We’ve Tried Everything”, Says Society That Has Only Tried One or Two Things.) The social sciences are still in their alchemical stage. We do not understand the fundamental workings of the human mind, let alone what happens when those minds combine in societies and economies. Imagine trying to cure cancer using Galenic medicine or trying to land on the moon using Aristotelian physics—that’s what we’re doing when we roll out programs designed to change human behavior.

That doesn’t mean our ill-informed attempts can never succeed. Both Galen and Aristotle were right about some important things: it was Galen who figured out that urine is produced by the kidneys, rather than the bladder (as was commonly assumed), and it was Aristotle who successfully described how objects move in fluids, even if he attributed it to the wrong forces.

But if we want to solve real, Hydra-headed problems, we need more than a handful of facts. (“Doc, I’m all itchy and covered in spots! What do I do?” “Hmm...did you know that urine is produced in the kidneys?”) Until psychology and its neighboring disciplines grow into scientific maturity, all we can do is guess and check. There’s nothing shameful in that, but there is something shameful in pretending otherwise.

This is hard for us to internalize, because by default we assume that we were born near the end of history. We understand, of course, that we still have a few things to figure out, but emphasis on the few. Just look at our beautiful universities, our begowned scholars, our numerous and inscrutable papers! How can you say we know nothing when we have so many TED talks?

We misunderstand what it feels like to be in the middle of things. Almost no one who read Galen or Aristotle ever thought to themselves, “oh, obviously this is only version 0.1 of our knowledge, all of this is tentative and incomplete, and one day it will be overturned and replaced with something better, something that actually works.” No, they thought to themselves, “Thank u Mr. Aristotle for your many true and useful facts.”

That’s why the worst possible reaction to a failed intervention is resignation. We may not know enough to improve our lot right now, but perhaps we could figure it out, if we tried. Maybe that means another RCT, or maybe it means another century of futzing around in the fundamentals before we can do anything useful.

(This does put a ceiling on the utopia we can expect to achieve in the near future. If you believe that we can perfect human nature by reorganizing society to your specifications, you would do well to remember that, as of now, we can’t even get people to go to the gym.)

That may seem unfair—what a bummer to be born in medias res, when so many of our problems remain unsolved! But if it is an affront, every human before us has been similarly affronted, and some of them chose to begin the work anyway. Whenever we pluck a low-hanging fruit today, it’s only because someone else planted a seed that they never got to harvest. So why should we expect to pluck without planting?

As Seneca put it nearly 2,000 years ago:

I revere the discoveries of wisdom and their discoverers [...] For me those things were acquired, for me they were labored for. [...] Let us make larger what we have received. Let this heritage pass from me to posterity increased.

I know some people don’t feel this way. Some believe that the answers are simple and known and merely need to be enacted by force. Others think the answers are unknowable and will remain so forever. For those folks, I offer an invitation: the next time we conduct the ritual before undertaking some new policy, they may have the honor of playing the part of the goat.

item.title: Google SWE points 48 AI agents at NASA Lidar, finds unmapped Maya pyramid in 72h (721 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://pietromiotti.com/latest/maya-site/?maya, See on Hacker News

5 min read

By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents discovered a Maya site in Mexico that, as far as anyone can tell, no one had reported before. It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive.

Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist.

I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part.

18 October

I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham, the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?"

I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar. From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath.[1]

So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya? Their region is much better covered by public lidar.

That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed.

19 October

I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses.

So how did they do it? They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide.

Me: That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives.

…a few hours later…

Agent: One major village doesn't seem to have been registered.

This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines.

Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir.

And this is what it looks like in 3D.

Me: OK, what should I do?

Agent: You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results.

Me: OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work?

Agent: …instructions for the report… + email addresses

Me: OK, please do the report.

And I went to bed.

20 October

I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one.

The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground.

Then I sent the report to INAH.

21 October

INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location.

To be clear, it's not official yet. But as far as anyone can tell, nobody had put this one on a map before.

So what was it?

This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an aguada, a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses.

I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then:

For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works (Cook et al. 2013) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology (Golden et al. 2016). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way (Auld-Thomas et al. 2024), others used lidar to estimate how many people lived in the Maya lowlands (Estrada-Belli et al. 2025), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces (Šprajc 2026).

What's next

In the report I offered to help with a field check led by INAH. In Mexico, archaeological sites are protected by federal law, and any fieldwork needs INAH's authorisation, so it's now up to the local INAH centre to decide whether to send a team. If they go, I'll post an update.

What I've learned

You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now.

And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute).

At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest.

  1. If you don't know how lidar works, copy and paste this prompt into your favorite AI tool: "Build an HTML page that explains how lidar works, with beautiful visualizations." ↩

item.title: Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card (172 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://blog.kate.land/posts/using-voltage-glitching-to-unlock-the-a100/, See on Hacker News

Summary

I’ve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, I’ve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards.
