Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I haven’t specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG.

Here’s how my “A100-80G” appears and functions.

NVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you more access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIA’s design allows one to relax restrictions by blowing more fuses!

In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. I’ve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here.

Acknowledgements

My work builds on prior research by Jon Pry and numerous others who have dedicated much of their time towards better understanding the GA100 die. I am disclosing my findings subsequent to another security researcher independently discovering the same vulnerability; I believe it to be in the best interest of the public to make this information publicly available. These findings were disclosed to NVIDIA’s product security team ahead of the publication of this article.

GA100 versions

The GA100 is an NVIDIA die that has been used to power almost 20 different SKUs - the A100 being the most well-known variant. I won’t delve into every SKU, but I will present the GA100 manifestations that matter to my work, covering the different versions of the CMP 170HX and the A100.

As fabbed, the GA100 die has 128 SMs, 12 FBPs, 5 NVDEC units, a PCIe Gen4 x16 controller, and depending on the framebuffer size, comes with 4-6 stacks of HBM co-packaged with the die. NVIDIA uses eFuses for yield-control and product segmentation–undifferentiated GA100s turn into more restrictive variants based on defect testing and manufacturer demand.

In one of the most extreme manifestations of product segmentation, the CMP 170HX, an Ethereum mining card with nominally 8 or 10 GB of application-exposed framebuffer capacity, actually comes with, respectively, ~80 and ~40 GB of HBM onboard! This work chiefly centers around how to fully unlock and use that capacity. Previous work has made great strides in unlocking the GA100 via software methods; VFI takes us across the last mile.

SKU Out-of-box Software (cmpunlocker) GA100VFI
CMP 170HX 8GB
Framebuffer 8 GB 64 GB 64-80 GB1
CMP 170HX 10GB
Framebuffer 10 GB 40 GB2 40-48 GB
Both CMPs
SMs 70 70 120-128
PCIe generation 1 2 4
NVLink No No Yes3
ECC No No Yes4
Multi-Instance GPUs No No Yes4
NVDEC 0 0 54

Hardware restrictions

So, how does NVIDIA utilize fuses to produce both a datacenter A100 and a mining CMP card from one die? To understand this, we need to take a closer look at the fuse controller located on the GA100.

The fuse controller is a block that contains 16,384 eFuses (512 rows of 32) and a bunch of logic surrounding that raw fuse macro. Its job is to perform fuse readout and programming, protect the underlying fuses, and provide usable “option words” to the rest of the die. These option words subsequently decide how the die functions and what features are enabled.

Each eFuse can be in one of two states (blown=1, unblown=0), and the 512 rows are divided into 4 regions:

  1. Regular fuses (rows 0-221). These are straightforward; often single (pairs of) fuses will map to an option word, such as OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM (an option word that determines whether further fuse programming is allowed or not). Regular fuses have built-in redundancy: for example, OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM consists of a PRI and RED (primary and redundant) fuse, in this case the primary instance is fuse 0 of row 0, and the redundant is fuse 0 of row 1. Some option words are scalars, such as OPT_X_COORDINATE, which is 9 bits wide and ostensibly holds the x-coordinate of the die on the fabbed wafer. Importantly, if a regular fuse is blown, there is basically no remedy to persistently unblow it (save for RIR later).
  2. Fuseless fuses (rows 222-487). This is a weird one. Apparently NVIDIA got frustrated with accidentally blowing regular fuses and ruining their engineering samples, and came up with a system to encode effective option words in a JTAG chain-like format (see this patent). Think about FF as essentially a script that describes what option words should have what values. FF fuses (excuse the RAS syndrome) concern most of the functionality we can unlock using VFI. This is because FF option words can be trivially cleared by simply writing new FF rows! We’ll about this more in depth, later. For now, you should know that NVIDIA also knows this, because under normal conditions, you are strictly prevented from performing any FF fuse blows.
  3. IFF fuses (rows 487-512). These contain instructions in a different format than the FF one. They’re out of scope for this post, and they’re mainly useful for on-the-fly reprogramming of fuse controller option words. They are usually not accessible in a production card.
  4. RIR fuses (8 rows of 32 fuses, which are technically not part of the 512 rows). These are provided by the designer of the fuse macro (TSMC datasheet here) and are essentially the first party designer’s intended “fuse repair” mechanism. The RIR section on a GA100 has space for 16 repair instructions, each overriding the value of an identified single fuse in the main 512 rows. Unfortunately for us, specifically in the 8 GB 170HX SKU, 15 of the 16 RIR words are all ones, and the 16th word encodes a useless repair instruction that can only be rarely leveraged for any interesting unlock. The story is different for the 10 GB SKU, but that’s a matter for another day…

There are two really interesting groups of fuses for the VFI-based unlock:

  1. “Control fuses”. The term comes from NVIDIA’s Tegra hardware headers, they use it to refer specifically to rows 0 and 1, which specify the values of highly security-sensitive option words.
  2. Fuseless fuses, which encode all of the interesting option words that decide whether a GA100 is born to be a measly mining card or an AI datacenter workhorse.

Before we name some of the FF-encoded option words, we’ll have to first understand the FF record format in a bit more detail, then talk about the die blocks that govern the features we are interested in.

Fuseless fuses

Each FF row is a 32-bit record. Bits 0–4 select a chain, bit 5 distinguishes FF from IFF (0 for FF), bits 6–15 select a 16-bit block, and bits 16–31 supply that block’s new value. The JTAG-chain picture from the patent is quite literal here: the controller builds the option data by replaying these records into chains. Fixed locations in each chain correspond to individual option words.

If two records address the same chain and block, the later record wins. For example, 0x0fe805c1 means chain 1, block 23, data 0x0fe8. Appending that record can clear an effective bit set by an earlier FF record. No physical fuse is unblown; a new row replaces the old 16-bit block. This works for FF-backed options, not the regular control fuses in rows 0 and 1.

Now that we know how FF words are encoded, here’s a list of the interesting words and their locations. These were discovered by a particularly helpful researcher who cross-compared FF values and effective option words from different GA100 SKUs in order to differentially understand the FF chain/block to option word mappings, as there is no known official mapping.

Named option Inferred FF location Use
NV_FUSE_OPT_FBIO_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 83–106; blocks 5–6 Memory I/O floorsweep
NV_FUSE_OPT_FBPA_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 107–130; blocks 6–8 Memory subpartition floorsweep
NV_FUSE_OPT_GPC_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 131–138; block 8 GPC floorsweep
NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC0_DISABLE through NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC7_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 187+8i through 194+8i for GPC i; blocks 11–15 Eight TPC masks
NV_FUSE_OPT_PES_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 251–274; blocks 15–17 PES floorsweep
NV_FUSE_OPT_FBP_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 307–318; block 19 Framebuffer partition floorsweep
NV_FUSE_OPT_ROP_L2_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 319–342; blocks 19–21 ROP/L2 floorsweep
NV_FUSE_OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 368–370; block 23 NVLink disable mask
NV_FUSE_OPT_DISABLE_GEN3_SPEED Chain 2 block 39; which of bits 1 and 9 is unresolved PCIe Gen3 speed restriction
NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_MAGIC_BITS_D[25] Chain 2 block 47 bit 3 Gen4 speed-disable flag
NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN23_DISABLE Chain 2 block 49 bit 6 PCIe boot policy
NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN3_DISABLE Chain 2 block 49 bit 7 PCIe boot policy
NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_DEVIDA Chain 2, bits 593–608; blocks 37–38 Device identity
NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_DEVIDB Chain 2, bits 609–624; blocks 38–39 Device identity
NV_FUSE_OPT_SYS_PIPE_DISABLE Chain 1, bits 372–379; block 23 Multi-instance GPU enabled pipes

The acronyms FBIO/FBPA/FBP/TPC/GPC/PES/ROP all refer to microarchitectural elements, please see this diagram from the GA100 whitepaper to further understand how these are related to each other:

FBP is the internal NVIDIA term for a “framebuffer partition”, with 2 FBPs to one HBM stack. FBPAs are subpartitions, 2 FBPAs to one FBP. PES/ROP are blocks (seemingly graphics-related) that are required for an SM to function.

With this knowledge in hand, what if we could write new FF rows that set the _DISABLE words to be all zeroes, or at least, as permissive as possible given die defects? If we look at how the _DISABLE options are used in conjunction with other elements, we’ll quickly see that these _DISABLE words are the primary lever we have in preventing parts of the die from being “floorswept”. After illuminating the “what-if”, I’ll talk about the “how”: the exact application of voltage fault injection and the fuse controller safeguards we can defeat with VFI.

Floorsweeping

NVIDIA puts these options in charge of setting floorsweep signals, which will render a die element unreachable (and likely powered down). From experiments, I believe the floorsweep lines are specified in RTL, emanating from the fuse controller and terminating in individual functional blocks and controlling some master power/clock domain switch within the block. I have observed the floorsweeping behavior to correspond with very little latency with the value of the fuse controller’s effective status words for each functional block.

Let’s take FBP floorsweeping, for example. On one of my 8 GB cards, OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852: FBPs 1, 4, 6, and 11 were masked. The separate OPT_FBP_DEFECTIVE mask was 0x840, covering 6 and 11. After I reduced the FF-backed disable mask to 0x840 with a replacement FF row, the extra masks on 1 and 4 were gone, but the defective 6 and 11 stayed disabled. That leaves 10 of the die’s 12 FBPs in the effective mask. Functionally, FBPs 1 and 4, which refused register reads and writes when OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852, became responsive after this fuse write.

Although the functional blocks can be “unfloorswept” with FF writes, this does not fully suffice to render the block fully available to an end application - the default framebuffer geometry configuration uses only a portion of each available HBM stack, for example.

To bypass that, we can utilize what is essentially a small modification to cmpunlocker’s method. The usual driver patch for the 8 -> 64 GB unlocks writes to a particular set of feature configuration words (FBPA_CFG, SM_SPEED_SELECT, etc.). The default values are chosen to succeed for the commonly found variant of the 170HX, which has the _DISABLE FF-derived option words preventing certain functional blocks from being used (any attempt to use them will return floorswept errors). With the unlocking FF burns in place, we can write even more permissive words into the configuration registers, resulting in what is functionally an A100-80G.

Achieving the FF burn

With the information we have, it seems straightforward that if one could blow arbitrary FF fuses, any GA100 could be fully unlocked to its maximum capability, as determined by die yield and the populated memory stacks. But how do we blow FF fuses? Let’s take a look at the fuse programming functionality of the fuse controller to understand more.

To request a fuse blow, one must write to the FUSEADDR, FUSEWDATA, and FUSECTRL registers belonging to the fuse controller. Although not nominally accessible to the host or to unprivileged requesters, with the Canary in the Crypto Mine ROP, opening up the responsible privilege level masks is trivial. And so, many researchers have attempted to coerce the fuse controller to blow fuses in the FF region. Some of our shared observations follow:

  1. The fuse controller has an internal FSM, and it indicates its current state via the FUSECTRL_STATE bits.
  2. The fuse controller enters a WRITE_PROGRAM state per each “hot” bit in the requested FUSEWDATA value. This tracks with the expected fuse programming behavior.
  3. However, unless a specific option word is cleared, writes to fuse addresses outside of the FPF range (rows 96-221) do not actually take place. Fuses in this region (believed to be “field programmable fuses” indicating a watermark of which ucode versions have run, alongside other field-relevant information) do take effect, and the fuse controller state machine behaves identically between FPF and non-FPF regions.

The specific option word I am referring to is OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE (“SBFE”), and it is set to be 1 in all production cards. When this option word is clear, fuse programming is allowed in any address. When it is set, only FPF fuses may be blown. To date, no one has found any way to burn FF fuses with SBFE=1, even when operating the fuse controller from HS contexts. It is not clear what “secured burn” truly means, I speculate that there must be a software-only way to perform non-FPF burns even with SBFE=1, and we just don’t know what the “secured” adjective really means here.

Note PLM, HS, ucode, …; I am delving into using a bunch of NVIDIA-specific terminology in this section as the explanation gets deeper. For a really in-depth explanation of what these mean, I refer you to other sources such as Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon.

Importantly, as people have figured out on more permissive cards, it is possible to perform FF burns with SBFE=0! And as it turns out, achieving this state is how we achieve the GA100 unlock. After much trial-and-error, I have resorted to inducing this state via voltage fault injection, and I was able to achieve it. Let’s talk some more about voltage glitching.

Voltage fault injection

Much has been said about VFI, and I’ll leave the in-depth explanation to other sources. In short, applying brief pulses of low supply voltage will often cause unexpected behavior in integrated circuits. I asked GPT-6 Astra to design an STM32G4 based board that taps into the PWMVID signal on the CMP PCB. PWMVID is an NVIDIA standard for voltage regulators, and my glitcher intercepts the PWM signal emitted by the GA100 die, and replaces it with its own waveform fed into the MP2888B VRM driver IC. With my setup, I can induce the card’s own VRM to produce timed glitches for me, which is simpler than MOSFET-based setups and enables faster glitching than attempting to directly drive the PMBus.

The glitcher requires two connections to the PCB, ideally done with magnet/enameled wire. One wire taps NVVDD for voltage sensing, and another wire taps the PWMVID signal. The only other required step for the glitcher to function is the removal of a 0402 0ohm resistor, which will break the connection between the GA100 output PWM pin and the VRM IC. Finding where to place the taps is trivial by tracing the pinout of the MP2888B, specifically its PWMVID and VOSEN pins (the MP2888B shares a footprint with its sibling public chip MP2888A). Test points directly adjacent to the MP2888B enable relatively easy installation of the PWMVID tap.

With this tap in place, a single glitch attempt involves this sequence:

  1. Remove card power
  2. Apply card power
  3. Start a timer (“glitch timer”) as soon as NVVDD crosses a threshold
  4. Execute a proposed voltage waveform by issuing a PWMVID signal, aligned to the glitch timer
  5. Observe card behavior, repeat from step 1 as needed

My setup achieves steps 1/2 with a simple ACPI S0 -> S3 -> S0 transition, which can be done in a few seconds on a modern desktop platform. More intrusive modifications or expensive rigs can probably achieve a better experiment rate, but in my experience this setup suffices to unlock cards in somewhere between 1 hour and 48 hours of glitching time using the approach described later.

For the NVVDD threshold, the Astra-authored firmware uses an STM32 comparator to detect when NVVDD crosses 225mV, after which a tight DMA loop drives the desired duties on the PWMVID pin. After S0, the host inspects the card state and decides what to do next; if it involves another glitch, the glitcher board will be commanded over USB with a glitch pattern. Then the host induces S3 with an RTC timer to wake back up in ~3s (empirically derived period for decent stability).

Sometimes the host will fail to return to S0, I’ve remedied this with relegating bookkeeping and glitch campaign preparation to an SBC (Radxa Cubie A5E) which also can drive the motherboard power/reset button pins via GPIO if the glitch target host is unresponsive.

More specifics are shared in the GA100VFI repository if you’re interested. For now, let’s take a look at the different interesting states we can trigger via VFI, as well as the specific glitch state that we need to burn FF rows. To help illuminate the differences between each glitch state, I have built an empirical model of how the fuse controller starts up when voltage is applied. Note that without the RTL that implements the fuse controller, all we have are guesses. Here are the hypothesized boot stages:

  1. Sense RIR, as required by the fuse macro
  2. Sense (from fuse macro into readout register) control rows
  3. Latch control rows into control row-derived option words
  4. Sense remaining rows
  5. Latch regular fuse values into their option words
  6. Parse FF chain
  7. Latch FF chain values into their option words

These hypothetical stages are based on what I can actually read from the die: controller states, raw rows when CMD_READ works, the published option words, and whether the PRI ring can still reach the rest of the GPU. By looking at a few key values, we can tell glitch outcomes apart. Importantly, glitch patterns and outcomes are very much die-specific, so consider these example waveforms and responses to be just that, examples. Let’s take a look at 3 interesting glitch states.

1. All fuses sensed as zero

Some glitches make almost every published option word read as zero. In one captured state, 669 of 672 named option reads were zero; the other three were error responses. The controller’s CRC status was 0x00 (not parsed yet), the PCIe ID read as 2080 (the base GA100 PCIe product ID, does not correspond to a real retail product), and the GPU’s PRI ring was held in reset.

This state is consistent with a catastrophic failure on behalf of the fuse controller. The card comes up basically unusable, because almost all boot functions are disrupted by the all-zero state. However, interesting enough, the card trains at PCIe Gen4 natively! Some slightly altered variants may showcase sections of fuses being successfully latched, or containing garbled values instead of all-zeroes. I was not able to push any of these states towards an FF burn; in almost all of them the fuse controller is unreachable or dysfunctional.

2. RIR read disrupted

Reading the RIR data on the CMP 170HX 8GB reveals its exact effect: 15 noop repair instructions, and one write that changes the value of a fuse in row 18, whose option word we can monitor. Further, because the RIR sense is consumed internally by the fuse macro instead of directly by the fuse controller, we can observe a disrupted RIR latch by attempting to read the raw row - the observed bitflip remains consistent across the flipped option word as well as the raw fuse row. This sets an interesting chronological checkpoint in investigating die boot (RIR sense must happen prior to other fuse sensing), but is not a useful glitch in itself.

3. Goldilock’s glitch

The successful three-pulse state on my first card seemed to disrupt precisely the row0/1 based option words, while leaving other fuses and option words intact. In this state, all of the row0/1 derived option words are zero. The initial readbacks look like this:

Signal Initial readback
PCI ID and access 20c2; BAR0 and the PRI ring respond
FUSECTRL 0xe0040000 (IDLE)
CRC_STATUS 0x55 (both halves parsed without errors)
DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE 0
OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE 0
ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM 0
FUSECTRL/FUSEOPT privilege masks 0xffffffff for both
Raw rows 0 and 1 Both still 0x53557c3d, unchanged from before the glitch

At this stage, we are still not yet capable of issuing FF writes, because ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0. I am honestly not sure why ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM would ever be zero, given it’s 1 in retail boards, so this almost reads to me like a way to implement a glitch-detection canary (or at least it would be elegant to do so).

Fuse sensing happens one row at a time, with all 32 fuses powered for sensing with one line, meaning it is much more challenging for an attacker to make a single fuse appear as cleared or set. It would make sense, then, to include a “canary” fuse that disables security-critical features (like fuse burning) when it is cleared, because usually the attacker can only manipulate fuse sensing at the row granularity at most. So, when the row0/1 option words come up as all cleared, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0 stops us from burning any fuses.

However, take a look at what we have in this state: DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE=0. This word is normally 1, and it stops us from setting the EN_SW_OVERRIDE register to 1, which then lets us “shadow” most of the option words exposed by the fuse controller. Doing so involves writing to a register CTRL_OPT_*, corresponding to option word OPT_*, which then determines the effective value STATUS_OPT_*. This is what lets us shadow SBFE to be 0. But, even though we have DSOV=0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM turns out to be one of the option words that are impossible to shadow, even with DSOV=0. So it seems we’re stuck.

At least that’s what I thought, and I banged my head against the wall in this state for a while. Then I noticed that there is one fuse controller command I haven’t tried issuing yet: SENSE_CTRL. I had refrained from issuing this, because on the face of it it seems like all of the row0/1 (control fuse) derived option words would match their fused values, which would reset SBFE, turn off software option word shadowing, and leave us unable to fuse. To my surprise, when I issued this command, all of the control-fuse-derived options went to their fused value, except DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE, which remained 0!

With DSOV=0, we can trivially set SBFE to 0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM is 1 because it matches its fused value, and we are off to the races! One wrinkle remains in that FUSEWDATA may have a locked down PLM, but with DSOV=0, we can just write 0 to OPT_SECURE_FUSE_WDATA_WR_SECURE to set the PLM to be all-ones, opening host access for fusing.

At this point, all that’s left to do is to calculate _DISABLE words that match the _DEFECTIVE values for the features we are interested in, and issue FF burns. Note that the occupied FF space and defective bits differ per die, so each burn must be die-tailored.

End results

Framebuffer unlock

On 8 GB cards with 80 GB intact (seems to be around ~90% of 8 GB cards from my limited sample size), the unlock yields the full 80 GB as a usable framebuffer. Multiple synthetic tests (writing pseudorandom words throughout the full framebuffer and reading them back after L2 invalidation) as well as real workloads (such as vLLM and SGLand) are fully functional. As mentioned, one of my cards has only 64 GB intact. In this case, the hardware unlock yields no framebuffer advantage.

Compute unlock

The 170HX is limited to 70 SMs out of the box. In practice, there are almost always >120 SMs non-defective on the die, and the unlock allows using them all. This results in a significant performance uplift, ~1.7x compared to the software-only 170HX unlock, and even an impressive ~1.2x over a retail A100!

PCIe generation

The only thing that stops cmpunlocker from advancing beyond PCIe Gen2 are the FF option words. With relevant bits cleared, Gen3/4 train and are confirmed to be fully functional. When combined with the PCIe decoupling capacitor mod, up to PCIe Gen4 x16 is attainable, matching a retail A100 PCIe variant.

NVLink

Zeroing out the OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE word is only one of the required mods for NVLink to actually work. Because the CMP 170HX PCB is missing the U11 IC (which connects PCIe 3.3v to an NVLink bridge pin), a stock board fails to bring up the reference clock generator on attached NVLink bridges. Simply bridging two of the pins on the footprint of U11 resolves this issue, although it removes whatever regulation or protection was provided by U11. Be careful if you’re bridging GPUs powered by different power supplies, as this will connect the +3.3V rails together unless you leave U11 unpopulated on some of your GPUs! The NVLink bridge works fine if you just patch U11 on one of the boards in the pair.

On the firmware side of NVLink enablement, there is a ROM check that needs to be bypassed with additional host-side commands. I’m sure your clanker can figure it out ;)

While investigating the NVLink unlock, I also found a few interesting quirks with NVIDIA’s NVLink implementation on the GA100. I will be posting a further blog post on this, so stay tuned!

Future directions

With arbitrary fuse burning, we mostly gain feature unlocks. Some security-sensitive options are shipped unblown by default, and burning them may lead to interesting footholds. But what’s more interesting to me are the deeper glitch states where many default-blown security-sensitive fuses sense unblown, enabling routes like debug HS execution, which grant unprecedented access to die internals.

References

  • Jon Pry, A Canary in the Crypto Mine: Defeating Stack Protection in a GPU Secure Coprocessor (2026).
  • Amogh Munikote, cmpunlocker (2026).
  • Otto Bittner et al., The Forgotten Threat of Voltage Glitching: A Case Study on Nvidia Tegra X2 SoCs (2021).
  • NVIDIA, US9230678B2: Integrated circuit having an enhanced fuseless fuse structure (2016).
  • TSMC, TEF07F32X32HD18_PHRM_C180518 electrical fuse datasheet, rev. 120A (2018).
  • hexkyz and SciresM, Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon (2021).
  • TechPowerUp, NVIDIA GA100 GPU specifications.
  • GA100VFI source repository.

  1. Anecdotally, out of the 10 specimens of CMP 170HX 8 GB I have examined, only one has shipped with only 64 GB usable, the rest all have a functional framebuffer size of 80 GB. ↩

  2. Although the Canary in the Crypto Mine paper claims a stable 80 GB on the 10 GB SKU, very few, if any, cards in the wild have been able to achieve this, and solid evidence is scarce. It remains plausible that some number of 10 GB SKUs really do come shipped with 80 GB on-board, however the percentage seems very low according to the community. Most “unstable” 80 GB unlocks are explained with a combination of L2 caching and memory aliasing over a true 40 GB framebuffer. ↩

  3. Enabling NVLink further requires a very small hardware mod due to a missing component on the 170HX PCB, I’ll talk more about this later. ↩

  4. Untested. ↩ ↩2 ↩3

item.title: Greg Kurtzer's Ginux is now a userspace kernel (111 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux, See on Hacker News

Ginux is a configurable userspace kernel for isolated Linux compatibility instances. It runs as an ordinary Linux process and places an explicit, versioned contract between managed workloads and the host kernel.

Important

Ginux began as an independent Rust kernel that booted directly through UEFI and ran a Rocky Linux 10 userspace. That research phase is complete. Its final source is permanently preserved on the bootable-kernel branch and at the bootable-kernel-final tag. Active development now continues here as a userspace kernel.

Why the project changed direction

The standalone-kernel experiment proved that an AI coding agent, directed by an experienced human through architecture, gates, and executable tests, could construct a new kernel capable of running meaningful Linux userspace. It also made the limits of that result obvious.

Linux is much more than source code. It is a stable interface, a development process, a global community, vendor and hardware alignment, and decades of compatibility and operational experience. Reimplementing kernel mechanisms does not reproduce that ecosystem, and competing with Linux was never the goal.

The more useful result is the boundary the experiment exposed. Linux must preserve a broad userspace ABI; as Linus Torvalds put it, “And we simply do not break user space.” The kernel regression documentation records that rule. Ginux can sit above Linux and deliberately offer a smaller contract to each managed instance. Before a managed syscall has a host effect, Ginux decides whether to emulate it, perform a validated mediated operation, or deny it.

Put bluntly: Linux must not break userspace; Ginux is designed to break the full Linux ABI guarantee deliberately and selectively. A instance receives only the capabilities and interface behavior its approved workload requires. Every departure is intended to be explicit, versioned, reviewable, and tested, rather than accidental incompatibility.

This pivot is also a result of the development method. AI made it practical to build disposable but executable prototype code, test an architectural idea, learn from the running system, and carry the valuable parts into a better design. The prototype was evidence, not an obligation to turn every experiment into a product.

What Ginux is now

Host Linux kernel
  `- host systemd (real PID 1)
       `- ginux (ordinary trusted host process)
            `- instance contract
                 |- virtual processes and identities
                 |- virtual descriptors and kernel views
                 |- assigned devices and resources
                 `- managed Rocky Linux userspace
                      `- instance systemd (virtual PID 1)

Ginux supervises native x86-64 programs and intercepts managed syscalls before their host effect. Its central dispatcher resolves the instance contract and chooses one of three outcomes:

  • Emulate: answer entirely from Ginux-owned state.
  • Mediate: validate and translate the request, then perform a narrow Ginux-owned host operation.
  • Deny: return a configured Linux-compatible error or terminate the task.

The current implementation includes:

  • a security-focused x86-64 interpreter and a balanced native ptrace backend;
  • strict, versioned instance configuration and lifecycle;
  • a digest-pinned OCI root, immutable filesystem index, and bounded overlay;
  • Ginux-owned process, credential, signal, synchronization, timer, and event models;
  • virtual devices with explicit assignment, ownership, and revocation; and
  • bounded virtual /proc, /sys, cgroup v2, mount, namespace, machine, and boot-identity views;
  • a host-shared network backend that remains syscall-mediated; and
  • a pinned Rocky Linux 10 systemd baseline that reaches multi-user.target, authenticates a managed console login, updates through Rocky's enabled repositories, and shuts the instance down cleanly.

This is a named compatibility baseline, not a claim of complete Linux or systemd compatibility. Its exact image, readiness marker, tests, evidence, and limitations are recorded in hdae/gates-todo/9-systemd-baseline.md.

Agent containment research

Ginux is also being tested as a containment boundary for AI agents and other automated software that can execute commands, modify files, open network connections, and start additional processes. Instead of giving an agent the host's complete Linux ABI, an operator can place its process tree inside a instance whose kernel contract exposes only the operations and virtual resources required for the task.

The research goal is a reviewable boundary spanning syscalls, ioctls, filesystems, devices, networking, process authority, and virtual /proc and /sys state. For example, a contract may allow an agent to read time, inspect its own processes, and modify one assigned workspace while denying clock changes, host filesystem access, unapproved network listeners, and unrelated devices. Ginux can then audit the contract decisions made while the agent and its child processes run.

This is an active verification target, not a claim that Ginux is currently a production-grade agent sandbox. The contract inventory, configurable policy, adversarial tests, performance costs, and escape boundaries are tracked through the HDAE gates and must be demonstrated before stronger containment claims are made.

Relationship to other systems

The userspace-kernel idea is established research and engineering territory. Ginux explores a particular point in that design space:

Approach Primary boundary Difference in emphasis
Linux seccomp Filters host syscalls Restricts the existing ABI rather than defining a complete virtual contract
User-Mode Linux Runs Linux as a host process Reuses a complete Linux kernel over virtual hardware
gVisor Implements an application kernel in userspace Closely related model with different compatibility and performance goals
Gramine Packages applications with a library OS Uses manifests and a library-OS boundary
Proxos Routes calls between private and commodity OSes Makes trust placement configurable across the syscall interface
Ginux Gives each instance a versioned kernel contract Treats the declared contract, virtual state, devices, resources, and lifecycle as one reviewable boundary

Ginux does not promise the complete Linux ABI. Compatibility claims apply only to named contracts, workloads, and executable evidence.

Development and testing

The reference development environment is macOS arm64. QEMU TCG boots a pinned Rocky Linux 10 x86-64 host where Ginux runs as an ordinary unprivileged process. The host systemd remains real PID 1.

Check prerequisites:

Prepare the pinned assets with explicit network operations:

make host-image-fetch
make image-helper-fetch
make instance-image-fetch
make systemd-image-fetch

Build and run the deterministic suite offline after the caches are populated:

make build
make check
make test

Inspect the latest completed capability directly:

make test-systemd       # cached image, external networking disabled
make bench-prepare      # one-time networked setup for the pinned benchmark image
make bench              # matched native/Ginux matrix plus mandatory budget checks
make bench-modes-prepare # one-time setup for the three-way dispatch comparison
make bench-modes        # native/selective/paranoid tables and graphs
make demo-gate-15       # bounded reproducible three-way comparison
make test-systemd-live  # shared network plus real upstream dnf -y update
make host-run           # general interactive Rocky host with Ginux installed
make host-reset         # discard that host's cache, instances, and writable state
make demo-gate-9        # Gate 9 checkpoint through the same host workflow

Instance recipes select syscall control under [contract.syscalls]:

[contract.syscalls]
control = "selective" # default; use "paranoid" for all-syscall mediation
default = "deny"
allow = ["*"]
deny = []

selective is the default and permits direct host execution only when the instance contract allows the operation and Ginux's versioned catalog independently classifies it as direct-safe. Denials, virtual state, inspection, translation, emulation, pointer or descriptor validation, and modified results remain Ginux-dispatched in both modes. paranoid is an explicit opt-in that sends every syscall through the Ginux userspace dispatcher before completion.

make bench-compare checks every row against the 4% native budget and, after an accepted baseline is published under benchmarks/gate11/, against that Ginux baseline as well. Environment mismatches are reported separately from performance regressions. make demo-gate-11 runs a bounded human-inspectable comparison and returns nonzero when a mandatory row misses its budget.

Gate 15 provides a separate characterization workflow across native Rocky, selective Ginux, and paranoid Ginux. Native is the no-mediation control, not a Ginux instance mode. The checked-in templates under benchmarks/gate15/ fix the complete test protocol and may be copied without editing scripts. make bench-modes produces paired raw samples, metadata, a Markdown table, and an SVG graph under build/gate15/. See Reproducible performance measurement for the exact protocol, customization workflow, output schema, and interpretation limits.

make host-run boots the QEMU Rocky host and logs you into its ordinary shell. Ginux is installed in PATH. The first create or import downloads and verifies the pinned Rocky OCI image with live per-layer progress; later operations reuse the cache. The writable Rocky host overlay persists across make host-run, ordinary cleanup, builds, and tests, so cached images, instance definitions, roots, and stopped status remain available. make host-reset is the explicit destructive operation that stops the host and removes that overlay; the next make host-run starts from the pinned clean Rocky image. A complete first session is:

ginux create rocky
ginux list
ginux status rocky
ginux start rocky --attach

create starts from the documented default recipe. Use ginux import NAME FILE to create or atomically replace an instance from a self-contained recipe, ginux export NAME to print that recipe, and ginux edit NAME to validate and atomically apply an editor session.

Instances are contract-locked by default. For an explicit maintenance window, stop the instance, run ginux unlock NAME, perform the required maintenance, stop it again, and run ginux lock NAME. ginux list and ginux status NAME show the current state, and starting an unlocked instance prints a warning. Unlocking relaxes configurable recipe restrictions only; Ginux still owns the virtual kernel boundary, rejects unsupported authority, reduces host identity, and applies NoNewPrivs. Lock state is host deployment state and is never written into an exported portable recipe.

Syscall auditing is disabled by default with [audit] enabled = false. Add --audit to ginux start to enable it for that run, or set enabled = true to enable it for every start. Enabled audit records always go to the instance's audit.log; they are kept separate from the attached console. Existing recipes using mode = "stderr" or mode = "disabled" remain read-compatible and normalize to the new boolean form when rewritten.

The instance specification supports typed recipe overrides, ingress and egress contract policy, volumes, virtual identity, and ordered pre-boot hooks. Host network attachment and translated ports are deployment settings, supplied as repeatable flags when the instance is created or changed:

ginux import web /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml \
    --network eth0:1 \
    --forward protocol=tcp,external_port=8080,instance_port=80 \
    --forward protocol=tcp,external_port=8443,instance_port=443
ginux set web \
    --network default \
    --forward none

Omitting --network uses the host's default network. Multiple flags are validated and persisted atomically; an invalid combination changes nothing. Hooks run only as mediated instance processes; Ginux does not support arbitrary host-context hooks. See Gate 9.75 instance specification for the schema, precedence rules, examples, and verification targets.

The same instance file contains a self-contained hierarchical contract under [contract] and its syscalls, filesystem, network, devices, privileges, process, and kernel subsections. Syscall names accept bounded globs compiled against the pinned catalog; explicit denies always win. The contract is part of the instance rather than a separate operator object. Validate and inspect the complete instance recipe before launch:

ginux validate /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml
ginux inspect /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml
ginux explain /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml filesystem.path.write

See Self-contained userspace contract for the syntax, precedence, migration behavior, and complete CLI workflow.

The attached terminal becomes the Ginux instance console. Log in as root with password ginux, explore normally, press Ctrl-] to detach while leaving the instance running, and run kill -RTMIN+4 1 as instance root to shut down systemd and return to the host. Detached operation uses ginux start rocky, ginux status rocky, and ginux stop rocky. Exit the Rocky host shell to stop QEMU cleanly. This stops the VM without deleting its persistent overlay; make clean resets that host state. make demo-gate-9 uses the same operator workflow; make run-systemd remains as a compatibility alias, and make test-systemd-interactive is the automated regression.

The live test and interactive demonstration enable shared external networking. An upstream DNF update can take many minutes under QEMU TCG because every managed syscall is intercepted and audited. The offline systemd test uses only the prepared, digest-pinned cache.

Individual component and gate targets are documented in the Makefile and the corresponding files under docs/ and hdae/.

Security model and limitations

The primary adversary controls a process inside an instance. The host kernel, hardware, Ginux executable and approved configuration, boot chain, and operator are currently trusted. The balanced native backend still relies on the host for ELF loading, address spaces, page faults, signals, scheduling, and ptrace; those remain host-kernel attack surface.

Ginux is research software. It has not received independent security certification, does not provide complete Linux compatibility, and is not ready for production workloads. Unknown contract operations fail closed, but current coverage and guarantees are limited to the tested gates.

The precise supported claims, retained supervisor authority, trusted components, exclusions, compatibility gaps, performance limitation, and reproducible boundary tests are documented in Security boundary and limitations.

For agent containment, the protected object is the host and any authority not explicitly assigned to the instance. Ginux constrains the Linux processes in which an agent and its tools execute; it does not inspect model reasoning, secure an external model provider, or make untrusted code safe outside the enforced instance boundary.

The full intent, threat model, invariants, and gate plan live in:

  • hdae/PROJECT.md
  • hdae/ARCHITECTURE.md
  • hdae/PLAN.md
  • hdae/STATUS.md

Development method

Ginux is developed with Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE): human-owned product intent, architecture, constraints, and acceptance boundaries combined with agent-executed implementation, diagnosis, and test loops. Each approved gate records its scope, non-goals, acceptance criteria, verification, evidence, and stopping point in hdae/.

Historical standalone kernel

The independent bootable kernel remains available for research and historical reference:

  • final branch: bootable-kernel
  • final tag: bootable-kernel-final
  • technical report and DOI

It is no longer the active development line. The code remains available under the repository's existing terms for anyone who independently chooses to study or fork it.

The name remains a joke in the same family as Linux: Ginux combines Linux, GPT, and Greg. To keep the author's ego within its configured resource limit, the G officially stands for GPT.

License

Ginux is available under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE.

Configured native launch

On x86-64 Linux, ginux launch <config> <root> [--result-file <fresh host path>] executes [instance].init with the configured arguments and environment inside the supplied host root directory. The bootstrap requires chroot and credential change privileges, and a kernel with close_range (Linux 5.9 or later). It drops to UID/GID 1000 before executing the workload. The configuration must select profile = "balanced" and backend = "ptrace-native"; storage and device assignments are not implemented by this command and are rejected.

[instance].workdir is optional and defaults to /work; / is also supported. The bootstrap creates the working directory if its parent exists, then enters it after dropping privileges. Init and working-directory paths are limited to 128 bytes and must be absolute without .. path components. Up to seven arguments of 128 bytes each and eight NAME=value environment entries of 256 bytes each are accepted. Invalid or oversized input fails before launch.

Workload stdout stays separate from supervisor diagnostics on stderr. Only stdin, stdout, and stderr are inherited by the workload. The launcher returns the workload exit code, or 128 + signal for signal termination. Startup failure returns 2; supervision or result-writing failure returns 1. Native fork, clone, and subsequent exec are unsupported; fork returns ENOSYS until child supervision is implemented. Non-x86-64 syscall ABIs and job-control group stops fail explicitly. Audit output is capped at 64 KiB plus a truncation notice. This path does not implement resource quotas from the instance metadata.

When requested, the result file is reserved exclusively before launch, with mode 0600 and a maximum path length of 512 bytes. Existing files are never overwritten. After completion, it contains one synced JSON object:

{"version":1,"outcome":"exited","code":0,"signal":null,"generation":null}

outcome is exited, signaled, or supervisor-error; only the relevant code or signal is populated. Storage generations are not implemented, so generation is null. A missing, empty, or malformed result is a protocol failure. A failure to write, sync, or close the result returns 1 even if the workload succeeded. Consumers should wait for launcher completion before reading it.

The focused Linux integration scenario consumes existing binaries:

make build
make build-launch-fixture
make build-gate1-fixture
sudo make test-gate1-setup
sudo make test-launch
sudo make test-native-supervision

Native process scenarios

The separate process-native <config> <executable> command exercises native fork, clone, vfork, exec, threads, waits, termination signals, and pipes. It executes a trusted host fixture as the caller, without chroot; it does not require root on a host that permits tracing child processes. Configured launch remains a separate entry point and does not yet use this process loop.

Process creation returns virtual identities, including clone TID cells. Untraced, reparenting, namespace, and unsupported clone flags are denied. Thread slots are reclaimed on exit. CLONE_FILES shares one descriptor table; ordinary fork copies it, and exec unshares it before closing CLOEXEC entries. Worker-thread exec preserves the group's process identity. Inherited host files above stderr are closed before execution. PI futex operations and queries for another task's robust list are unsupported.

Build the fixtures explicitly, then run their independent scenarios:

make build build-process-fixtures
make test-process-native
make test-process-native SCENARIO=shared_pipe
make test-process-native SCENARIO=thread_exec

The scenarios consume existing binaries under .artifacts/process, including checks for syscall ABI dispatch, clone restrictions, descriptor inheritance, thread reuse, successful and failed worker exec, signals, wait-status writes, nonblocking waits, and vfork. The existing native fork fixture also runs. These checks do not claim complete libc, job-control, or systemd compatibility.

item.title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS (118 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/adrbn/bo2-mac, See on Hacker News

Call of Duty: Black Ops II, statically recompiled from 32-bit x86 Windows to native ARM64 macOS.
Campaign, Zombies and multiplayer against bots, built on your Mac from your own Steam copy.

English · 中文

       

Why · Abstract · Method · Limits · Repository · Legal
Beta, 2026-11-03 · measured on one Apple M1 (4 performance + 4 efficiency cores, 16 GB)


Campaign (Angola), Zombies (Town) and multiplayer (Hijacked, against bots) on an Apple M1, recorded while playing; the number in the top right corner is frames per second, and the screen recording itself costs some, mostly in the campaign. 80-second video (MP4, 20 MB)

Important

This repository contains no game file and no translated game code. It turns your own Steam copy of Black Ops II into an app for your Mac, on your Mac. The game's code ends up inside that app, so nobody can hand you a ready-made one: each player builds their own, and it may not be shared. Unofficial fan project, not affiliated with Activision, Treyarch or Microsoft. To play, buy the game. Beta: read what has and has not been proven.

Why

Black Ops II never came out on Mac, and on Apple Silicon it was not really playable before. AppleGamingWiki lists it as unplayable under CrossOver and not supported under Rosetta 2. What remains is a Windows ARM virtual machine in Parallels, with reports ranging from 1 frame per second in matches on an M1 Max to 60–80 on M3 and M4 (MacGamingDB). Here the game is translated once, before it starts, into a native ARM64 app: 51–60 frames per second on a base M1, with no Windows and no virtual machine. Being native also means it can be fixed and extended like any Mac app: split-screen, which the PC version never had, is in progress.

Abstract

bo2-mac takes the three executables of Black Ops II, the campaign (t6sp.exe), Zombies (t6zm.exe) and multiplayer (t6mp.exe), and turns their x86 machine code into ARM64 machine code ahead of time. Remill lifts each function to LLVM IR, a chain of our own passes rewrites that IR, and the result is linked with a Win32 runtime written by hand, whose Direct3D 11 is drawn by Metal. There is no Wine and no JIT: the game runs as native code, in one process. About 150,000 functions are translated across the three executables. Only the short sequences that the copy protection hides run in a small x86 interpreter, and so does any code the translation missed, so a hole is built to cost speed rather than crash the game.

On an Apple M1 the campaign runs at 51–60 frames per second, and every mission loads and hands over to the next one, down to the end credits. Zombies is played solo on six maps through the game's own menus at 57–60. Multiplayer is played against bots through its real menus, eleven game modes, at 53–60. One app, Black Ops II.app, opens the campaign, and the CAMPAIGN / ZOMBIES / MULTIPLAYER entries of each menu switch to the other game.

Nothing is downloaded from anyone but you: the converter reads the executables of the copy you bought, checks them byte for byte, and builds the app on your machine.

Results

measured conditions
Campaign 51–60 fps every mission loads and chains to the end credits; not all played end to end
Zombies 57–60 fps (Die Rise 43–58) TranZit, Mob of the Dead, Nuketown, Origins, Buried, Die Rise, solo, through the real menus
Multiplayer against bots 53–60 fps eleven game modes through the real menus: a full round, the scoreboard, back to the lobby
Game world against real time ≈ 1.0× the game's own server clock against wall time
Conversion on the player's Mac about 1 hour 45 on an M1 (the campaign alone: about 45 minutes) the campaign is playable as soon as it is converted; Zombies and multiplayer follow
Disk peak about 10 GB, about 4 GB kept after the conversion, only the linked binaries stay

Frame rate counts the drawables really presented to the screen, checked against the screen and the Metal HUD.

What you can play


The real main menu: NEW STORY, RESUME STORY, REPLAY MISSION. From angola to the end credits, the missions load and hand over to the next one. Strike Force missions start with a click.
The six maps, solo: main menu, lobby, match, Game Over, scoreboard, then another match in the same process. DLC maps play if your Steam account owns them.
Custom Games against bots from the real menus: CHOOSE CLASS, the HUD, a full round, the scoreboard and back to the lobby. The match rules are this project's own script.

All three modes: keyboard and mouse, or a DualSense as XInput through GameController.framework; sound on; movement keys follow their position on your keyboard (ZQSD on AZERTY, WASD on QWERTY), unless you bound them yourself in the game's options.

Pipeline

In five steps, all on the player's Mac:

  1. Check. The converter accepts only the exact Steam build of each executable, checked by SHA-256. The launcher asks the Steam client on your Mac whether the signed-in account owns the game, and refuses otherwise.
  2. Catalogue and lift. Ghidra lists the functions of your own executable; Remill v6.0.1 lifts each one to LLVM IR. Five patches to the lifter are carried in tools/remill-patches/, among them the x87 rounding mode, and one that forks a running Remill for each function instead of reloading its x86 semantics.
  3. Fold. Remill's IR is correct but slow: every guest memory access, flag and x87 push is a call or a store into a State structure. Our passes rewrite it before clang -O2: guest reads and writes are inlined, lock sequences become hardware atomics, the guest ret stays inside the lifted code, and the x87 stack is promoted to locals.
  4. Runtime. runtime/ implements the Windows imports the game really calls, with exact stdcall arities (the Steam API ones taken from Valve's public headers). Guest memory is one 4 GiB mapping. Direct3D 11 is a fake-COM layer over Metal; DXBC shaders go through HLSLcc. XAudio2 goes to CoreAudio, and the videos are decoded natively with libvpx.
  5. Threads. Guest threads start as coroutines on one host thread, which removes most sources of non-determinism and makes a run replayable. The fast configuration moves the server, the render backend, sound mixing and decoding, and the job workers onto real host threads. ARM is not TSO, so this needed real memory barriers.

The copy protection is executed, not bypassed. The game hides integrity checks behind hardware exceptions, single-step traps and code it decrypts into the heap. A small x86 machine built on Unicorn (x86_guest_vm.cpp, heap_code.cpp) runs exactly those sequences and hands control back to the recompiled code. No check result is forced and no key is placed by hand.

A hole in the translation is built to cost speed, not a crash. When the game reaches x86 code that was never lifted, the same machine runs its original bytes (interp.cpp) and gives control back to the recompiled code at the next translated block, call or return. Each interpreted address is logged ([INTERP]).

The online service is answered locally. Zombies and multiplayer expect Demonware; a responder written from the game's own requests (dw_local.cpp) answers the lobby, storage and ticket on your Mac. Nothing leaves the machine.

Why not Wine, CrossOver, DXVK or DXMT?

They translate Windows calls at run time and keep the x86 code under Rosetta. Here the x86 code itself is gone: it is ARM64 machine code before the game starts. DXVK and DXMT are PE DLLs that reach their native backend through Wine's unixlib mechanism; this port has no Wine, and its Direct3D 11 is its own layer over 32-bit guest memory. Only shader translation was needed from outside, and HLSLcc, a plain C++ library, covers it.

Findings

Each entry is a symptom seen on screen, the cause that was measured, and the effect of the fix.

Thirteen findings, from the x87 rounding mode to a false start inside one instruction

F1 · The lifter ignored the x87 rounding mode. In Zombies the prone view shook. fistp rounded to nearest where the game had asked for truncation, inside the network codec of the view height. The height received by the client was wrong on 8 samples out of 8, and on 0 out of 8 after a Remill patch and a re-lift of the codec.

F2 · One reserved bit of the x87 control word. A campaign mission froze in an effects loop, only with real threads. The lifter stored bit 6 of the control word differently from real hardware. A one-line Remill patch and four re-lifted runtime functions fixed it, with no slowdown.

F3 · A CPU feature flag changes the algorithm. Our IsProcessorFeaturePresent answered "no SSE2", so the C runtime took its x87 ceil, which rounded to nearest under our runtime. An effect then sampled index −1 forever: two missions froze.

F4 · Our own log caused the stutter. Hitches of 170–430 ms were the render thread blocked in write(): our log, redirected to a file on a nearly full disk. Sending it through a pipe to a child process took the hitches per run from 12 and 8 to 0 and 0.

F5 · Shader translation moved constants by 4 bytes. HLSLcc placed a float2 after a float at offset 24 where Direct3D reads it at 20. 31 of 2,664 shaders were affected, among them the eyes and the reticles.

F6 · The protection has to run. The options menu froze 8 times out of 8. An integrity check rewrites its own return address to point at code decrypted into the heap, which the runtime ignored. Running that code, as Windows does, gave 3 out of 3 without a freeze.

F7 · Our own safety guards were the obstacle. One guard of ours stopped the game at 28 seconds of play. The largest gains of the project came from removing our own guards and false sharing, not from clever code.

F8 · An empty API stub looks like a broken service. Two stubs that returned nothing (CryptGenRandom, StringFromGUID2) looked like a network failure in Zombies.

F9 · Thread priorities are part of the program. SetThreadPriority was a stub. Passing the mixer's request to macOS cut the short audio buffers of a run from 908–1872 to 7–71, and the sound gaps with them.

F10 · Native skinning, bit for bit. CPU skinning rewritten in NEON gives the same bits as the original x86 and took a heavy scene from 17.8 to 30.3 fps.

F11 · Decals need the game's depth bias. Scorch marks and blood appeared or vanished with a slight turn of the camera. The game asks for a depth bias on decals; our layer left it at zero. Passing the game's values to Metal fixed it.

F12 · The render thread was copying the level's geometry every frame. In multiplayer and Zombies it copied 23–63 MB of vertex data to the GPU per frame, most of it static. Keeping static buffers resident in Metal brought the copies to 3.5–5 MB per frame: multiplayer 51.8 → 60 fps, Zombies 43.1 → 58.2. The same change does nothing in the campaign, where the pace is set by the scheduler thread. A speed-up helps only the mode whose bottleneck it touches.

F13 · A false start inside one instruction cost half the frame rate in combat. In the first conversions from a fresh Steam copy, Zombies fell to 25 fps whenever the player fired. Hot functions were running in the interpreter: the catalogue placed the start of the next function inside the first instruction of a root, so its bounded sweep decoded zero bytes and the root was dropped without a word. Sweeping such roots without the bound, as the one-by-one lifter already did, put them back in the translated code.

Method

Predict, then measure.

  • A prediction is written before the result is read: about 1,100 numbered ones by the time of this beta.
  • At least three runs per configuration. Run-to-run noise is 30–64%, so a difference under about 40% cannot be seen at n = 3.
  • A change must prove it is active: the log has to show it firing.
  • A run that never reaches the level is a dead run, not a data point.
  • The screen beats the log. When the screen contradicts a probe, the probe is wrong.
Record and replay, retractions, clean room, who does what

Deterministic record and replay. With every guest thread a coroutine on one host thread, most sources of non-determinism are gone; the replay is checked against the recording, not assumed. Three boundaries capture all outside input: the import dispatcher, the window message drain, and the consumed audio buffers. The journal is about 16 MB. It allows the same run twice with exactly one flag changed.

The instrument is the thing that fails. Nearly 200 findings were taken back along the way. The largest share (31%) were an instrument that answered a different question; the next (17%), one that could not answer at all. So every oracle here names its input and refuses to answer when that input is missing.

Clean room for the match rules. Multiplayer and Zombies take their match rules from a daily patch file that Steam no longer ships. The replacement in runtime/match_rules/ was written by a team that never saw the original script: one team wrote a behavioural specification from the game, the other wrote the code from that specification alone, and the two only spoke through written questions and answers, kept with their dates.

Who does what. AI agents supply the throughput: writing the shims, bisecting millions of calls per run, reading tens of thousands of lines. The human supplies the goal, the corrections from what is really on screen, and refuses the flattering conclusion. This is one game, months of work and heavy manual intervention.

Limits

  • Local only. Multiplayer and Zombies run against the responder on your Mac. There is no online play, no LAN and no co-op yet. League Play is refused.
  • Match rules are ours. Written in a clean room (see Method); behaviour may differ from the original in places.
  • Heat. The Mac runs very hot during long sessions (111–116 °C reported on the M1). Play plugged in: on battery, macOS throttles the game hard. Plugging in avoids the slowdown, not the heat.
  • First game on each map. In Zombies and multiplayer, shaders are translated for Metal while the map loads, so that first load is longer and the first minute can still hitch slightly. In the campaign they are translated when they first appear, so the loading cinematic stays smooth and the first pass through a place can hitch. Everything is cached: the next time, it loads fast and runs smooth.
  • Window. The game runs in a 1280×720 window.
  • Other Macs. Only one M1 has been measured. M2, M3 and M4 should be faster, but no number is claimed.
  • Campaign. Every mission loads and chains; not every one has been played end to end.
  • Zombies. Grief and Turned need a second player, and there is no co-op yet.
  • macOS audio. When the system's coreaudiod is unhealthy the campaign stalls on its first video. Check that afplay -t 1 /System/Library/Sounds/Tink.aiff takes about 1 s; restarting the Mac fixes it.

Install

You need an Apple silicon Mac, macOS 14 or later, at least 20 GB free (the conversion peaks at about 10 GB and about 4 GB stays), Homebrew, and Steam for Mac signed in to the account that owns the game.

git clone https://github.com/adrbn/bo2-mac.git && cd bo2-mac
brew install llvm@17 cmake ninja libvpx unicorn
pip3 install capstone
scripts/make_app.sh --from-source

Open Black Ops II.app, point it at your game folder and let it convert: about 1 hour 45 on an M1, the campaign first in about 45 minutes. The campaign is playable as soon as it is converted: play it then, and Zombies and multiplayer are converted when you first pick them in the game's menu. Otherwise the conversion goes on through all three. If the disk falls under 8 GB free, the conversion stops cleanly and resumes where it was.

Updating, or if the conversion stops. Run git pull && scripts/make_app.sh --from-source in the repository folder: what is already converted is kept and the conversion resumes. An update redoes only what its changes touch: a fix to the runtime relinks the three modes in about 3 minutes on an M1 instead of converting again. If it still fails, open an issue with the log it names.

The converter only accepts the exact Steam build, checked by SHA-256. The Steam executables are encrypted by Valve's SteamStub wrapper and this repository provides no way to remove it: the converter expects the three decrypted images in ~/.bo2-native/steam/ (t6sp.exe.unpacked.exe, t6mp.exe.unpacked.exe, t6zm.exe.unpacked.exe). You make them yourself from the copy you bought, with a separate tool of your choice. Only the wrapper must go: the file names above and the SHA-256 check tell you at once whether a file is right. Never share these files.

DLC. The launcher asks your Steam client which DLC your account owns, exactly as the game does on Windows. A DLC map plays when you own it and its files are in your game folder.

Repository

path what it holds
runtime/win32/ the Win32 runtime: kernel32, the scheduler, Direct3D 11, sound, input, the local service responder
runtime/gfx/ the Metal backend: presentation, shader cache, render targets
runtime/match_rules/ the clean-room match rules for multiplayer and Zombies
tools/ the lift driver, the catalogue, the IR passes, the disassembly and analysis tools
tools/remill-patches/ the patches carried on top of Remill v6.0.1
scripts/ make_app.sh, the Steam installer and converter, the launchers
third_party/HLSLcc DXBC to Metal shader translation
docs/ the prerelease status, the toolchain

Roadmap

  1. This beta: the three modes from a fresh Steam copy, on other Macs than the one that built them. Your reports (Mac model, frame rate, what broke) decide what comes next. First outside report, 2026-11-05: on an M2 Pro (16 GB), the conversion completed and the game started, after three fixes found on the way (#4, #5, #6).
  2. No Terminal: one app to download and open, then drop the game folder on its window. It carries its tools already built, so nothing is compiled on your Mac but the game itself (macOS 26 or later; macOS 14 and 15 keep the Terminal install).
  3. Fully translated: the 46 code blocks that still run through the Unicorn interpreter are translated ahead of time, and every translated instruction is checked against the interpreter; any translated function can be sent back to the interpreter, to find a wrong one by halving.
  4. No shader wait: shaders built before the first match, instead of at launch (about 3 minutes in multiplayer) and during play (freezes when a new effect appears). Started: shaders now compile in batches, and the ones from the last sessions compile in the background at launch. In multiplayer on an M1 without Xcode (a few tries, not a benchmark), shader compiling during the first two minutes of a match went from 18–25 s to 10–14 s on a first launch and about 5 s on the next one; freezes over 300 ms went from 15–22 to 13–15, then 7. The first launch still freezes about as often.
  5. Shorter conversion: down from about 2.5 hours to 1 hour 45 on an M1 (2026-11-06, measured on all three modes: the preparation reads the executable once, the lift and the fold use every core the memory allows). An update now redoes only what changed (a runtime fix: about 3 minutes). Next: less optimisation for code that rarely runs. The three modes share only 4 % of their functions, so converting shared code once would gain little.
  6. Faster, without heat: the campaign is bound by the scheduler thread, not by rendering; multiplayer with 11 bots is bound by the server thread. Native rewrites of the hottest functions come next, then frame rates above 60 for 120 Hz screens.
  7. Controllers: vibration and aim assist.
  8. Together: real UDP sockets for Zombies co-op, Grief and Turned, and multiplayer over LAN. Then local split screen, which the PC version never had: two copies of the game drawn in one window, one controller each, joined over that LAN.
  9. Later: MetalFX, post-processing when the frame is presented, and replacement textures loaded from the player's own copy.

Legal

For a copy the user owns, on hardware the user owns.

  • No engine source and no leaked code are used.
  • Neither the input binary nor the recompiled output is distributed. No game file is included: the player needs their own Steam copy of Call of Duty: Black Ops II. The converter only accepts the exact Steam build (SHA-256), and ownership is checked each time the game starts by the player's own Steam client: the game refuses to run when Steam is not signed in or the account does not own it.
  • The copy protection is executed as the game wrote it; nothing in it is patched out. This repository provides no way to remove Valve's SteamStub wrapper.
  • The online service the game expects is answered by a local responder written from the game's own requests: no Activision server is contacted, there is no online play, and game ownership is still checked by the player's Steam. The match rules were written in a clean room.
  • The code written here is licensed under GPL-3.0 (LICENSE).
  • Unicorn (GPL-2.0) is linked statically from Homebrew when you build (tools/boot.py). GPL-2.0 and GPL-3.0 code cannot be shipped together in one binary, so the prebuilt tools of roadmap step 2 cannot embed Unicorn as it is linked today. Building from source on your own Mac is not affected.

This is an unofficial fan project. Call of Duty and Black Ops are trademarks of Activision Publishing, Inc. Steam is a trademark of Valve Corporation. This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Activision, Treyarch, Microsoft or Valve. To play, buy the game.

item.title: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave (352 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://gatezh.com/posts/macos-secure-enclave-ssh-keys/, See on Hacker News

I’ve been paranoid about my SSH keys for a while now. They just sit there in ~/.ssh/, protected by nothing but file permissions. Any malicious script that gets access to my filesystem could just copy them and get into all my servers. Also, there have been many stories out there online about fake interview assignments that asked to clone a repo and run it on your local machine. This is one of the reasons I switched completely to using devcontainers, but even that was not really enough for me (and it shouldn’t be enough for you or anybody else really).

So I finally decided to do something about it.

TL;DR

I have decided to NOT go with the native macOS Secure Enclave approach (using only out-of-the-box tools) because it ended up plain ugly and I can’t live with that. However, it is a fully functional, working solution that I would definitely use otherwise.

The Options

After some research, I found several ways to protect SSH keys:

  • Native macOS Secure Enclave — no third-party apps, built into the OS
  • Secretive — third-party app that stores keys in Secure Enclave
  • YubiKey — hardware security key with FIDO2 support
  • 1Password / Bitwarden — store keys in an encrypted vault, use their SSH agent

I already use 1Password, but I might switch to something else in the future. Bitwarden recently added SSH key support (even on the free tier!), but it’s still a software solution — the keys are encrypted at rest but decrypted in memory when used.

What I really wanted was hardware-backed security. The private key should literally be impossible to extract, even if my Mac is fully compromised.

That left me with YubiKey or Secure Enclave. I have a YubiKey 5C, but I wanted to try the native approach first — no extra hardware to carry around, no third-party apps to maintain.

What is Secure Enclave SSH?

Since macOS Sequoia (and Tahoe), macOS supports SSH keys backed by the Secure Enclave, a security subsystem on the Mac’s chip that is isolated from the main processor. The private key is created inside it and never leaves.

When you SSH somewhere, your Mac asks the Secure Enclave to sign the authentication challenge. If you enable Touch ID, you have to approve each signing operation. The actual private key never exists in memory or on disk.

The workflow is surprisingly similar to regular SSH keys:

AspectRegular SSH KeySecure Enclave Key
Where private key lives~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (a file)Secure Enclave
What’s on diskActual private keyJust a reference (useless without this Mac)
Setup on remote serverCopy public key to authorized_keysSame
ConnectingJust worksTouch ID prompt, then works

Setting It Up

Step 1: Create the Secure Enclave Key

macOS provides the sc_auth command (Smart Card Authentication) to manage CryptoTokenKit identities. Despite the name, it works with Secure Enclave too.

sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-MacBook" -k p-256-ne -t bio

Breaking this down:

  • -l "ssh-MacBook" — a label for your reference (only visible locally)
  • -k p-256-ne — NIST P-256 curve, non-exportable (the key can never leave Secure Enclave)
  • -t bio — require biometric (Touch ID) for every use

You’ll be prompted for Touch ID to create the key.

Problem 1: Touch ID Error

When I first ran this command, I got a scary error:

Error: Error Domain=NSOSStatusErrorDomain Code=-25293 "Failed to generate keypair"
(errKCAuthFailed / errSecAuthFailed: / Authorization/Authentication failed.)
UserInfo={..., NSUnderlyingError=... "Failed to get bio catacomb UUID for user 502." ...}

Turns out my Touch ID enrollment got reset somehow. After re-enrolling my fingerprint in System Settings → Touch ID & Password, the command worked fine.

You can verify the key was created:

sc_auth list-ctk-identities

Output:

Key Type Public Key Hash                          Prot Label       Common Name  Valid To          Valid
p-256-ne A71277F0BC5825A7B3576D014F31282A866EF3BC bio  ssh-MacBook ssh-MacBook  2027-01-26, 10:18 YES

Step 2: Export the Key Handle

Now we need to create a “key handle” file that SSH can use. This is NOT the private key — it’s just a reference that tells SSH “go ask the Secure Enclave to sign this.”

ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N ""

When prompted for PIN, just press Enter (it’s not used for biometric keys). Touch ID will pop up. This creates id_ecdsa_sk_rk and id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub in your current directory.

Move them to your SSH directory:

mv id_ecdsa_sk_rk* ~/.ssh/

Step 3: Configure SSH to Use the Secure Enclave Provider

Add this to your ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc):

export SSH_SK_PROVIDER=/usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib

Reload your shell:

Problem 2: Outdated Commands Everywhere

If you search for “macOS Secure Enclave SSH” online, you’ll find a lot of guides telling you to run ssh-add -K. Don’t. It’s deprecated:

WARNING: The -K and -A flags are deprecated and have been replaced
         by the --apple-use-keychain and --apple-load-keychain
         flags, respectively.

And even the new flags don’t work for Secure Enclave keys — they’re for the traditional macOS Keychain, not CryptoTokenKit. The SSH_SK_PROVIDER environment variable is the correct approach.

Step 4: Get Your Public Key

cat ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub

Output:

sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh:

That ssh: at the end is the FIDO2 application ID — it’s part of the key, not a comment. You can add your own comment after it when copying to authorized_keys:

sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh: macbook-secure-enclave

Step 5: Copy to Your Server

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub user@your-server

Or manually paste the public key (with your comment) into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.

Step 6: Configure ~/.ssh/config

Problem 3: SSH Doesn’t Find the Key

After setting everything up, I tried to SSH… and it asked for my password.

The verbose output (ssh -vvv) showed SSH was only trying my old RSA key:

debug1: Offering public key: /Users/sergii/.ssh/id_rsa RSA SHA256:...

The problem: SSH doesn’t automatically look for files named id_ecdsa_sk_rk. It only auto-discovers standard names like id_rsa, id_ed25519, id_ecdsa.

The fix is to explicitly add it to your ~/.ssh/config:

Host *
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

SSH tries identity files in order, so put the Secure Enclave key first if you want it to be the default.

⚠️ Note: If you’re using 1Password’s SSH agent (IdentityAgent), it might conflict with this setup. I had to comment it out while testing.

Step 7: Test It

You should get a Touch ID prompt, then connect.

The Ugly Touch ID Prompt

One thing I’m not thrilled about: the Touch ID dialog says “ctccardtoken needs to authenticate to continue” instead of something friendly like “SSH wants to use your key.”

This is because the prompt comes from CryptoTokenKit — a low-level framework that Apple hasn’t polished for end-user SSH. If this bothers you, Secretive provides a much nicer UI while still using Secure Enclave under the hood.

Why Touch ID for Everything?

I initially thought about creating two keys — one with Touch ID for “important” servers, one without for convenience (like Git operations).

But then I realized: without -t bio, malware could use my key silently. With -t bio, I always know when something is using my SSH key. A few extra taps per day is a small price for that visibility.

So my recommendation if you’re planning to store your SSH keys this way: just use -t bio for everything. If it ever gets annoying, you can always create a second key later.

The Catch: No Backups

Secure Enclave keys are tied to your specific Mac. If your Mac dies, the keys die with it.

That’s by design: the key can’t be exported, so it can’t be backed up either. Keep more than one key instead. Add your Secure Enclave key AND a backup key (from a YubiKey, or another Mac) to your servers’ authorized_keys. If one device is lost, you still have access via the other.

Final Thoughts

It seems to be a proper way to store your SSH keys securely, and it is way better than storing them on your hard drive.

With the implementation above you get:

  • ✅ Private key literally cannot be stolen (it’s in hardware)
  • ✅ Every SSH operation requires Touch ID (I know when my key is used)
  • ✅ No third-party apps needed
  • ✅ Works with existing authorized_keys workflow

However, I’ve been somewhat surprised by the ugliness of the UI. Not sure why Apple released such an unpolished thing. In each and every presentation they have a section on security (where their Apple logo becomes an Apple lock), so I was expecting an actual aesthetically appealing look for their security features. It is definitely not the case. My sense of beauty is not compatible with this ugliness, so I will be looking into other solutions to store my SSH keys in Secure Enclave such as Secretive.
